course.title: Psychology: How Minds Work
course.description: Detect a faint signal, watch a memory fade and recover, and test the classic studies against their replications.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with percentages, square roots and simple algebra. No previous psychology or statistics course is assumed.

paragraphs: Psychology is the scientific study of how minds work and why people think, feel and act as they do. Claims about people are hard to test, because people vary, forget things, guess what a study is about and see patterns that are not there. Learning how the field copes with that is the best way to judge what it says about sleep, memory or why a crowd stands by while someone needs help.

The course has twelve lessons in four parts. The first part, How we know, covers what a correlation can and cannot show, why random assignment makes a fair comparison, and how to tell a big effect from a lucky one. Perception and attention looks at detecting faint signals, at what attention hides, and at how the mind combines cues. Memory and learning covers holding things in mind, forgetting and spaced retrieval, and conditioning. Thinking and the social mind finishes with base rates, anchors and fast intuition, and conformity, obedience and bystanders.
Each lesson explains first and asks afterwards, and most put numbers on an idea so that you can check the result yourself.
outcomes: You'll be able to say why a correlation does not show a cause and name other explanations for it.
You'll be able to judge how big a research finding is and how many people a study needs to find it.
You'll be able to separate how well someone detects a faint signal from how readily they say yes.
You'll be able to work out how likely a positive result is to be right once the base rate is counted.
You'll be able to explain how forgetting, conditioning and the pull of a crowd shape what people remember and do.

lessons.title: Correlation is not a cause

lead.text: The clerk's lists are easier to read as a picture. Draw a sheet with the day's takings along the bottom and its rescues up the side, and put one dot for each day where its two figures meet. A day with big takings and many rescues lands far to the right and high up. A day with small takings and few rescues lands near the bottom left.

In the town's picture the dots climb from the lower left to the upper right. This pattern, where two measures tend to rise and fall together, is called a correlation. Because both measures rise, it is a positive one.

afterFigure.text: The second picture shows the opposite pattern. People were asked how many hours they had slept and then timed on how quickly they reacted to a light, and the dots slide downhill. Reaction time is a time, so a smaller number means a quicker person. People who slept more were quicker, so one measure falls as the other rises. That is a negative correlation.
A pattern like this is easy to see but hard to describe exactly. The next screen gives a way to say how tight it is without waving a hand at the picture.

lead.text: A picture shows a pattern, but two people can disagree about how strong it looks. Statisticians settle that with one number, the correlation coefficient, written r. It is worked out from the dots, and it always lies between −1 and +1.

Two things about r matter. Its sign gives the direction. A plus sign means the measures rise together, as in the town, where r is +0.75. A minus sign means one falls as the other rises. Its size, with the sign ignored, gives the strength. At +1 or −1 every dot sits exactly on a straight line, and at 0 there is no line to see, only a cloud. The nearer r is to either end of the scale, the more tightly the dots follow a line.

afterFigure.text: Compare the two pictures. The town's dots hug a rising line, and r = +0.75. The dots for practice and test score are more spread out, and r = +0.4. Both slope upward, and the larger number marks the tighter pattern.
So r tells you which way the dots lean and how closely they follow a line. It says nothing about why they lean that way, and that question is where the rest of the lesson goes.

lead.text: Direction and strength are separate things. Use what the last screen said about each when you compare these two correlations.

Strength can also be put another way. The kiosk's takings change from day to day, and that spread is the variation in the takings. The rescues vary too. Where two measures are correlated, part of the variation in one goes along with the variation in the other.

To find out how large that part is, square r. The result is the share of the variation the two measures have in common, called the shared variation. With r = 0.4 the square is 0.4 × 0.4 = 0.16, so the two lists share 16% of their variation. The other 84% belongs to things that do not line up with the other list.

Squaring also removes the sign, because a negative number times itself is positive. A correlation of −0.4 shares exactly as much as +0.4, since direction has no bearing on how much two lists have in common. A correlation that looks respectable at 0.4 still leaves most of the variation unshared.
Here are the sleep and reaction-time dots again. The first picture has a correlation of r = −0.6.
Back to the clerk's records. Takings and rescues rise and fall together across the summer, and nobody has said why. Use what you know about a seaside town in summer.

The answer you chose is the most common reason two lists match when neither causes the other. On hot days the kiosk sells more ice cream, and on hot days the pool is crowded, so there are more swimmers and more chances for one to get into difficulty. Heat sits behind both lists and pushes them up together. A hidden variable that drives both measures like this is called a confound.
You can test for a confound by holding it still. The clerk also wrote down each day's temperature, and the first picture shades every dot by it. The high-takings, high-rescue days are the hot ones.

afterFigure.text: The second picture keeps only days of about the same temperature, between 21 and 23 °C. With the temperature held still, the upward lean has gone: higher takings no longer go with more rescues, and r falls from +0.75 to about 0.

So the kiosk was never sending anyone into the water, because the weather drove both lists. That is why a correlation alone cannot show a cause: the dots show a pattern, but what lies behind it may be a variable nobody wrote down.

lead.text: Confounds turn up wherever two measures both depend on something else, as both lists in the town depended on the weather.

A confound is one way to explain a match, and the direction of the link is another. When exercise and mood go together, it is natural to say that exercise lifts mood, but the numbers cannot confirm that. A correlation is symmetric: swap the two axes of the picture and r stays exactly the same.
The figure draws one study of exercise and mood both ways round, with r = +0.3 in each.

afterFigure.text: The data look identical either way, so nothing in them says which measure is the cause. People who feel good may be the ones who go for a run. Putting the arrow the other way, from mood to exercise, is called reverse causation. Both directions can even hold at once.
To separate them you would have to decide who exercises, instead of watching who chooses to. The next lesson is about doing exactly that.

lead.text: Each explanation below says something different about why exercise and mood go together.

The third way a match can arise is in the mind of the person looking. A driver says it always rains the day after he washes his car. He remembers the rainy times because they annoyed him, and he forgets the dry times, which he never gave a thought. To test his belief you have to count every day, not only the memorable ones.

Say he washed the car on 10 days and it rained after 4 of them. On the other 90 days it rained after 36. The counts are different sizes, so turn each into a percentage first: 4 out of 10 is 40%, and 36 out of 90 is also 40%. Rain followed a wash no more often than it followed anything else.

afterFigure.text: Believing in a link that the full counts do not show is called an illusory correlation. It grows from vivid cases, which are easy to remember. The cure is to count the dull cases too and compare rates in every group.

blocks.text: A seaside town keeps two sets of records through the summer. The ice-cream kiosk on the front writes down its takings each day. The lifeguards at the open-air pool write down each swimmer they have to pull out of trouble. At the end of the season a council clerk puts the two lists side by side and sees that they follow each other. The days with the biggest takings are the days with the most rescues, and the quiet days are quiet for both.

At the next meeting a councillor proposes closing the kiosk, since it seems to be sending people into trouble in the water. The clerk is not sure. A matching pattern in two lists is easy to see, but it does not say what produced it.

This lesson follows the clerk's records from the pattern itself to the question of what lies behind it. We start by drawing the pattern and putting a number on how closely two lists match. Then we look at the different ways a match can arise, some of which have nothing to do with one thing causing the other.

intro.promise: By the end you'll measure how closely two things move together and name three ways they can match without a cause.

recap.keyIdea: A correlation gives direction, strength and shared variation, but never the cause. A confound, a reversed arrow or a vivid memory can each produce a pattern that nothing causes.

blocks.text: Back at the seaside, the clerk has what the council lacked. Takings and rescues had r = +0.75, and with the weather held still the link vanished, so the kiosk can stay open. You squared r = −0.6 to find that sleep and reaction time share 36% of their variation, and you found that 6 of 20 and 30 of 100 are the same busy rate.

recap.nextHook: A correlation cannot say which explanation is right, but a study that decides for itself who gets what can, and the next lesson begins with a gym that lets its members choose.

lessons.title: Random assignment

lead.text: Start with the gym's own comparison. Members were free to join the programme or stay out, and the manager compared the two groups three months later. The trouble is that the groups differed long before the programme began. Someone who volunteers for a fitness programme is likely to be someone who already exercises, enjoys it and has the time.

So the joiners may have been fitter on the first day, and the gap three months on may come from that head start. When people sort themselves into groups on a trait that bears on the result, the effect is called self-selection. Here the trait is how much people already exercise, and it works as a confound built into the design, much as the weather did in the seaside town.
The next screen puts numbers on how large such a head start can be.
Eight members can choose. Four who exercise a lot choose the new programme, and the other four mostly stay away.

The repair is to take the choice away from the members. Write each name on a slip of paper, shuffle the slips and draw them. The first half go into the programme, and the rest form the control group, who carry on as before and give something to compare against. The draw does not care whether a member is keen or lazy, fit or unfit.

This is random assignment: every person has the same chance of landing in either group. The figure shows one set of twelve members, each with a score for how fit they were before the study, divided up three different ways by chance.

afterFigure.text: No draw makes the groups identical, and the three here differ by different amounts. What the draw guarantees is that no trait favours one group. A member who is fit, keen or short of time is as likely to be in one group as the other. That holds for traits nobody thought to measure, which is something no amount of careful choosing by researchers could promise.

lead.text: Random assignment makes the groups fair, which is a weaker thing than making them equal. Suppose the draw puts people with fitness scores 5, 9, 4 and 6 in group A, and people with scores 7, 3, 8 and 10 in group B. Group A adds up to 24, and 24 divided by 4 gives an average of 6. Group B adds up to 28, which gives an average of 7.

Group B starts one point ahead, and nothing has yet been done to either group. That gap is chance. Draw again and the gap changes, and sometimes group A will be the one in front. What matters is that the draw never leans one way: over many draws the gaps cancel out, and in larger groups each gap tends to be smaller.
A small study can still be unlucky. The remedy is more people in the groups, and the draw itself stays.
Two groups were drawn at random. Group B started with an average one point above group A, before anything was done to either group.

steps.headline: What you set and what you measure

lead.text: With fair groups in place, the gym still has to say exactly what it is comparing. In the study the researchers decide one thing: who gets the programme. That is the independent variable. Afterwards they measure an outcome to see whether it changed, such as each person's resting heart rate after three months. The measured outcome is the dependent variable, because its value depends on the condition.

The outcome also needs a precise meaning. Fitness is a loose word, and one researcher may take it to mean strength while another means stamina. An operational definition says exactly how a concept will be measured, such as the distance a person covers in a 12-minute run. Anyone could repeat that measurement and get comparable numbers.
Fixing these choices before the data arrive stops researchers from searching afterwards for some outcome that happens to differ.
Researchers assign people at random to a fitness programme or no programme. After three months they measure each person's resting heart rate.

Random groups and clear measures still leave one problem. People often improve simply because they expect to, and symptoms often fade with time anyway. If one group takes a drug and the other takes nothing, the drug group improves for three reasons mixed together: the drug, the expectation and the passing time.

The fix is to give the control group an identical-looking pill with no active ingredient, called a placebo. Now both groups expect to be treated and the same time has passed. The placebo group shows how much improvement expectation and time produce on their own, so only the extra improvement in the drug group can be credited to the drug.

Expectation can leak in a second way. If the people who measure the symptoms know who received the drug, their judgement can lean towards the result they hope for, often without their noticing. And if participants can tell which pill they were given, the placebo no longer keeps their expectations equal.

A double-blind trial closes both gaps. Neither the participants nor the people measuring them know who received the drug until the results are in. If only one of the two parties is kept in the dark, the trial is single-blind. Together with random assignment and a placebo, double-blinding leaves the treatment as the one difference between the groups.
The control group in a drug trial gets a pill that looks the same as the real one but has no active ingredient.
A drug trial gives one group the drug and another an identical-looking placebo. Both groups improve on a symptom score.

blocks.text: A gym lets its members choose whether to join its new fitness programme. Three months later the manager tests everyone and finds that the joiners are fitter than the members who stayed out. A friend says that proves the programme works, and the manager would like to put the figures on a poster.

The last lesson showed how a pattern can come from something hiding behind it, and the gym's comparison has that problem. The groups were not made fairly, and the result may say more about who joined than about what the programme did.

This lesson builds the test the gym should have run. We take the version it ran and repair it one flaw at a time. Each repair closes off a way for the result to mislead, until the only difference left between the groups is the programme itself.

intro.promise: By the end you'll explain why random assignment makes a fair comparison, and name the variables, placebo and blinding a fair trial needs.

recap.keyIdea: Random assignment gives everyone an equal chance of each condition, so no trait systematically favours one group. A placebo and blinding keep expectation equal, and the gap that remains is the treatment.

blocks.text: Back at the gym, you can now say why the manager's comparison could not be trusted. You found that volunteers began 6 hours a week of exercise ahead, and that a chance gap of 0.5 is no sign of bias. You also found that a drug's own effect is 12 − 8 = 4 points once the placebo response is taken away.

recap.nextHook: A fair trial can show that a programme made a difference, but not whether the difference is big enough to matter, and the next lesson begins with a training course that raised scores by 6 points in two very different classes.

lessons.title: How big, and will it replicate?

lead.text: Take the training course from the opening. In each class the scores are spread out, and nobody scores exactly the class average. Some do better than average and some do worse. The usual size of that scatter around the average is called the standard deviation. In class A it is about 3 points, so a typical student sits within a few points of the average. In class B it is about 30, so scores are all over the place.

The standard deviation matters because a gain only means something beside it. If scores wobble by 3 points anyway, a gain of 6 is a clear shift. If they wobble by 30, a gain of 6 is about what you would see between two groups of students who had no training at all. A change should be judged against the scatter in the scores.
Both classes gained 6 points on average from the course. Think about the scatter in each class.

That suggests a measure. Divide the gain by the standard deviation, and the answer says how many spreads the two groups have moved apart. In class A, 6 ÷ 3 = 2, which is two whole spreads. In class B, 6 ÷ 30 = 0.2, a fifth of a spread. This ratio is Cohen's d: the difference between two means (the averages) measured in standard deviations.

The figure draws each class's scores as a bell-shaped curve, one for the untrained group and one for the trained. Where d is 2 the two curves hardly overlap, and almost every trained student beats the typical untrained one. Where d is 0.2 the curves lie nearly on top of each other.

afterFigure.text: Because d counts in spreads, it lets you compare results measured in different units. Jacob Cohen suggested rough labels of 0.2 for small, 0.5 for medium and 0.8 for large, and warned that they are no substitute for knowing what counts as a worthwhile change in the field in question.

lead.text: A control group scores 100 on average and a training group scores 106. Scores in both groups scatter with a standard deviation of 15.

The d we have used so far assumed both groups scatter by the same amount. Often they do not, and one group may be tightly bunched while the other is loose. Dividing by the plain average of the two spreads would treat both groups as equally important, although the looser group says more about how unreliable the scores are.

The usual remedy is a pooled standard deviation. Square each group's standard deviation and average the two squares, then take the square root. Squaring makes a large spread count for far more than a small one, so the pooled value leans towards the looser group. When both spreads are equal the pooled value is just that spread, which gives a quick check on any working. Then divide the gap between the means by the pooled value, as before.

Average the two squares, then take the square root. This is the pooled standard deviation.
Divide the difference between the means by the pooled standard deviation.

steps.headline: The chance of finding a real effect

lead.text: Suppose the course really does help, with a true effect of d = 0.3. A study of a small group may still fail to show it, because a handful of students can easily be unlucky. Statistical power is the chance that a study detects an effect that is really there. A study with 80% power finds a real effect in 8 attempts out of 10.

Detecting needs a rule. A result counts as significant when, if there were no real effect, a gap this large would turn up by luck fewer than 5 times in 100. That 5% cut-off is written α = 0.05, and 80% power at α = 0.05 is the usual target.
Small studies have low power. They often miss real effects, and the few effects they do find tend to be lucky overestimates, because only an unusually big gap clears the cut-off in a small group.
A small study goes looking for a small effect, using a cut-off of α = 0.05.

steps.headline: How many people a study needs

lead.text: A study can be planned to have enough power. Lehr's rule of thumb gives the number of participants needed in each group for 80% power at α = 0.05: 16 ÷ d². For a large effect with d = 0.8, that is 16 ÷ 0.64 = 25 people per group.
Because d is squared, the number climbs quickly as the effect shrinks. At d = 0.5 the rule gives 16 ÷ 0.25 = 64 per group, and at d = 0.2 it gives 16 ÷ 0.04 = 400.

afterFigure.text: The two pictures show why. With d = 0.5 the curves are visibly apart. With d = 0.2 they overlap so much that it takes a crowd of participants to see the gap above the scatter.

lead.text: A team plans a study of an effect with d = 0.4. They want 80% power at α = 0.05.

steps.headline: A result that does not repeat

lead.text: A study finds an effect, and the next thing to ask is whether it holds up when someone else tries. A replication repeats the study with fresh participants. If the original effect was real, the repeat should find it again. If the original was a lucky draw from a small sample, the repeat will usually find less.

The Open Science Collaboration tested this by repeating 100 psychology studies. Of the 100 originals, 97 had been significant, but the repeats reached significance in only 35 of those 97 cases. Power posing, the idea that holding an expansive pose for two minutes raises testosterone, also failed to hold up when 200 people were tested.

Repeats carry most weight when they are large and preregistered, meaning the researchers published their plan, with the measures and the analysis, before collecting any data. They cannot then steer the result afterwards. A failed repeat of that kind counts for more than the original paper.
Ego depletion is the claim that self-control runs down like fuel. Published studies averaged about d = 0.6. A preregistered repeat across 23 laboratories tested 2,141 people.

blocks.text: A training course lifts test scores by 6 points on average. The organisers ran it in two classes. In class A, scores usually differ from the class average by about 3 points. In class B they differ by about 30. The single number 6 looks the same in both classes, and the organisers want to say how well the course worked.

The last lesson ended with a fair trial, which can show that a course made a difference. It cannot say whether the difference is big enough to matter, or whether anyone who repeated the study would find it again. Those questions run through this lesson.

We start with a way of measuring a gain against the ordinary scatter of scores. After that we look at how many people a study needs before a gain of a given size shows up reliably, and at what it means when a well-known result fails once other laboratories repeat it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll judge how big an effect is and how many people a study needs, and read a failed repeat as evidence.

recap.keyIdea: An effect is only as big as it is large next to the spread, which is what d measures. Small studies miss real effects and overstate lucky ones, so one result needs repeating.

blocks.text: Back with the training course, a 6-point gain gives d = 2 in class A and d = 0.2 in class B. You divided a 6-point gain by a spread of 15 to get d = 0.4, and found that an effect that size needs 100 people per group. A multi-laboratory repeat of ego depletion then gave d = 0.04, nowhere near the published 0.6.

recap.nextHook: So far the question has been whether a result is real, and the next lesson turns to measuring someone who must decide whether a faint signal is there, beginning with two guards who watch a car park.

lessons.title: Signal and noise

steps.headline: Four things that can happen on a night

lead.text: Take one guard on one night. Either a thief comes or none does, and either the guard shouts or stays quiet. That gives four outcomes. If a thief comes and the guard shouts, it is a hit. If a thief comes and the guard stays quiet, it is a miss. If no thief comes and the guard shouts anyway, it is a false alarm. If no thief comes and the guard stays quiet, it is a correct rejection.

Two of those outcomes are mistakes, and they are different mistakes. To measure each one we divide by the nights where it could happen. The hit rate is the number of hits divided by the number of nights a thief came. The false-alarm rate is the number of false alarms divided by the number of nights no thief came.

Guard A's records show how this works. A thief came on 10 nights and A shouted on every one, which is 10 hits out of 10 and a hit rate of 100%. Of the 10 quiet nights, A shouted on 9, so the false-alarm rate is 90%.
A guard is on watch on a night when a thief does come. Match what happens to one of the four outcomes.

steps.headline: Why even a careful guard gets it wrong

lead.text: A quiet night is never completely quiet. A shadow moves, a gate rattles in the wind, a car door slams down the road. Call everything that is not a thief noise, and call the thief the signal. A night's overall impression is stronger when a thief is there, but the noise varies from night to night, so the impressions are not fixed.

Plot how often each strength of impression occurs and you get two bell-shaped curves, one for quiet nights and one for thief nights. They overlap, because some quiet nights feel more suspicious than some thief nights. The guard has to choose a line along the scale: an impression stronger than this means shout. That line is the criterion.

afterFigure.text: In the figure, the part of the thief curve to the right of the line is the share of thief nights on which the guard shouts, which is the hit rate. The part of the quiet curve to the right of the line is the false-alarm rate. Because the curves overlap, no position of the line gives all the hits and none of the false alarms.

lead.text: The guard can move the criterion without getting any better at the job. Set the line low and the guard shouts at the faintest hint. Nearly every thief night is caught, and many quiet nights are shouted at too. Set the line high and the guard shouts only at strong impressions. False alarms become rare, and some thieves slip past unchallenged.

Moving the line changes both rates in the same direction, so every gain in hits is paid for with more false alarms. Look at the two pictures. The distance between the two curves is the same in both, since moving the line does not change how far apart the curves sit.

afterFigure.text: That distance is set by how much stronger a thief's presence makes the impression and by how well the guard senses it. It is the measure of skill, and the line is not. The next screens turn it into a number.

lead.text: Over twenty nights a thief came on ten of them. Think about the line each guard has set and about how often each one shouts on each kind of night.

The distance between the curves is called d′ (say d-prime), or sensitivity. We cannot see the curves, only the rates, so we turn each rate into a z-score. A z-score says how many standard deviations a position sits above the middle of its curve. The table is standard: a rate of 0.50 gives z = 0, 0.80 gives 0.84, 0.90 gives 1.28 and 0.954 gives 1.68. A rate below one half gives the same size with a minus sign, so 0.20 gives −0.84, 0.10 gives −1.28 and 0.07 gives −1.48.

Then d′ = z(H) − z(FA), where H is the hit rate and FA the false-alarm rate. Guard B shouted on 8 of 10 thief nights, so H = 0.80 and z(H) = 0.84. B shouted on 1 of 10 quiet nights, so FA = 0.10 and z(FA) = −1.28. Subtracting a negative adds its size, so d′ = 0.84 − (−1.28) = 2.12.
A large d′ belongs to a guard who catches most thieves and rarely raises a false alarm. If the shouting ignores what is actually happening, d′ is near zero, even when many thieves get caught.

steps.headline: Find d′ when the hit rate has z = 1.28 and the false-alarm rate has z = −1.28.

lead.text: Another guard has a hit rate of 0.80 and a false-alarm rate of 0.20. The table on the last screen gives their z-scores.

Skill is half the story. The other half is where the guard puts the line, and that is measured by the criterion, written c. It is found from the same two z-scores: c = −[z(H) + z(FA)] ÷ 2. If c is 0 the line sits midway between the two curves. A negative c means the line sits low and the guard says yes readily. A positive c means the line sits high and the guard is cautious.
For Guard B, z(H) = 0.84 and z(FA) = −1.28, so the sum is −0.44. Halving it gives −0.22, and the minus sign in front turns that into c = +0.22. Guard B leans very slightly towards caution.

The two measures answer different questions. Training and practice raise d′. Costs and rewards move c: a guard who is blamed for every missed thief will lower the line, and one who is blamed for waking the street will raise it.
A guard starts shouting more readily because missing a thief has become costly.
A baggage screener flags a bag at the faintest hint of danger. Missing a weapon would be far worse than a delay.

blocks.text: Two guards watch the same car park overnight. Whenever one of them thinks a thief is about, that guard shouts. Over twenty nights a thief really came on ten of them. Guard A shouted on all ten of those nights, and also on nine of the ten quiet nights. Guard B shouted on eight of the ten thief nights and on one quiet night.
Each guard looks good in one way. Guard A never lets a thief through, and Guard B rarely wakes the street for nothing. A single score for how good a guard is would hide that difference.

The same puzzle turns up wherever someone must decide whether something faint is really there, such as a radiologist reading a scan or a screener checking a bag. This lesson takes the guards' records and pulls apart two things that are easy to run together: how well someone can tell a real event from the background, and how ready they are to say yes.

lessons.title: Where attention goes

lead.text: Start with something you have probably done. You are reading in a café when someone at the next table begins an interesting story, and a minute later you realise you have read the same line three times. Your senses were taking in the page the whole time. Your attention was somewhere else.

At every moment your senses take in far more than the mind can use. Attention is how it chooses. It follows one stream, such as the story at the next table or the line you are reading, and turns the others down. This is selective attention, and it is what lets you follow one voice in a noisy room.

The choice has a price. What you are not attending to is dealt with far less thoroughly than what you are attending to. How far that can go is shown by an experiment that has been repeated many times.

In the experiment, viewers watched a short film of two teams passing basketballs, one team in white shirts and one in black. They were asked to count the passes made by the white team. Partway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the middle of the players, thumped their chest and walked out again. The gorilla was on screen for several seconds.

When viewers were asked afterwards whether they had noticed anything unusual, around half had not seen the gorilla at all. They were not careless or short-sighted. Many had counted the passes accurately. Their attention was on the white shirts and the ball, and an object in plain view, which they did not expect and were not looking for, never registered.

This is inattentional blindness: failing to notice a clearly visible, unexpected object because attention is directed at something else. Looking at a thing and seeing it are different, and attention is what links the two.
Here is a class demonstration with the same film. The counts show how many of the people counting passes missed the gorilla.

Now return to the eight cards. Call the sums task A, in which you judge whether a digit is odd or even, and the word puzzles task B, in which you judge whether a letter is a vowel or a consonant. Every trial takes some time. When you move from A to B, or from B to A, the mind has to drop one set of rules and pick up the other, and that takes extra time called the switch cost. Repeating the same task has no such cost.

To count the switches in a sequence, look at each pair of neighbouring trials and count the pairs where the task changes. The first trial is not a switch, because nothing came before it. AAB has one switch, between the second A and the B. ABAB has three.

The total time for a sequence is the number of trials times the time per trial, plus the number of switches times the switch cost. The figure shows two orders of eight trials with the same trial time and the same switch cost.

afterFigure.text: The alternating order has a switch between every pair of neighbouring trials. The blocked order has just one, in the middle. Both orders contain the same work, and the difference in time comes entirely from the switches.

lead.text: Read a sequence from left to right and compare each trial with the one before it.

steps.headline: Find the time for AABAB when each trial takes 400 ms and each switch adds 100 ms.

workedSteps.text: Five trials, each 400 ms.
Count the changes of task: A to B, B to A, A to B.
Each switch adds 100 ms.
Add the trial time and the switch time.

lead.text: Now use the digit and letter judgements from the cards. Each trial takes 600 ms, and each change of task adds 200 ms.

The two orders of the eight cards have the same number of trials, so the time spent on the cards themselves is the same. Only the number of switches differs. Doing the sums first and the words after, in the order AAAABBBB, has a single switch. Alternating has one between every pair of neighbouring trials, and each of those switches adds the same cost.

People can reduce a switch cost by getting ready. If you know which task comes next, you switch faster. Preparation shrinks the cost without removing it, which is why answering messages while writing a report takes longer than it feels. Each message is a switch away from the report, and the return to the report is another.
Each trial takes 600 ms and each change of task adds 200 ms. Both orders contain eight trials.

The same cost appears outside the laboratory. Driving is a task, and so is working through a problem in your head. A driver who does both is not doing them at the same instant. Attention moves between them, and each move is a switch.

Watson and Strayer asked whether anyone escapes this. They put 200 people in a driving simulator and gave them a demanding memory-and-arithmetic task to do while they drove. They then checked whether either task got worse compared with doing it alone.

For nearly everyone it did. A very small group, whom the researchers called supertaskers, showed no measurable cost on either task. Because supertaskers are so rare, a person who feels sure they multitask well is much more likely to be one of the others.
Some drivers in the study showed no cost at all from doing a second demanding task. The counts are in the picture.

This lesson starts with what happens when attention is pointed hard at one thing, including a failure that happens in plain view. Then it returns to the cards and puts a price on every change of job. It ends with a study of people who tried to do two demanding things at once while driving.

lessons.title: Perception as inference

steps.headline: One sense gives a wobbly reading

lead.text: Start with sight alone. You look at the block and your eyes give you a number, say 50 mm. Look again after blinking and you get 49, and the next look gives 52. The readings gather around the true height, yet no single look is exact. Over many looks they average out near 50 mm and typically stray from that average by about 2 mm.

That typical stray is the standard deviation, or SD, the usual size of a scatter around an average. A small SD means the readings bunch tightly, so one look is nearly as good as any other. A large SD means they are scattered, so any one look could be well off.

Every source of information about the world wobbles in this way and has an SD of its own. Psychologists call such a source a cue. Sight is a cue to the block's height. Touch is another. Because no cue is exact, working out the height is a matter of inference: a best guess drawn from the evidence you have.

Now put on the thick gloves and feel the block. Your fingers say 56 mm. Gloves dull the sense of touch, so these readings wobble more than the ones from your eyes, with an SD of 4 mm against sight's 2 mm.

You are left with two readings, 50 mm and 56 mm, which cannot both be exact. One way out is to split the difference and say 53 mm. That treats the two cues as equally good, and whether they are is the real question.

Think of two friends giving you directions. One has lived in the area for years and the other visited once. If they disagree you would not give them equal say. You would lean towards the friend whose directions have turned out right more often, while still listening to the other. The mind faces the same choice with every pair of senses, and it makes it with a rule that can be written down.
Sight reads the block at 50 mm and its readings wobble by an SD of 2 mm. Touch through the gloves reads 56 mm with an SD of 4 mm. You have to give one best estimate of the height.

steps.headline: Weighing cues by how steady they are

lead.text: The steadier cue should count for more, and there is a precise way to say how much more. Give each cue a number for how far it can be trusted, called its reliability, and set it to 1 ÷ SD², where SD² means the SD multiplied by itself. A cue with an SD of 1 mm has a reliability of 1 ÷ (1 × 1) = 1. A cue with an SD of 3 mm has a reliability of 1 ÷ (3 × 3) = 1/9. Because the SD is multiplied by itself, a cue that wobbles more loses reliability quickly.

Each cue's weight is its share of the total. Add the reliabilities, then divide each cue's reliability by that total, so that the weights add up to 1. The combined estimate is the weighted average: multiply each reading by its weight and add the results.
The figure shows a second, shorter block. Sight reads 30 mm with an SD of 1 mm, and touch reads 36 mm with an SD of 3 mm. The taller, narrower curve belongs to the steadier cue.

afterFigure.text: The combined estimate, marked in teal, sits close to the sight reading. If both cues were equally steady they would get equal weights, and the estimate would fall exactly halfway between them. The midpoint is a special case, correct only when the cues are matched.

lead.text: Reliability depends on the SD multiplied by itself. Work it out for a cue with an SD of 2 mm, and again for the same cue after its SD has grown to 4 mm.

steps.headline: For a second, shorter block, sight reads 30 mm (SD 1 mm) and touch reads 36 mm (SD 3 mm). Find the combined estimate.

workedSteps.text: Find each cue's reliability, 1 ÷ SD².
Divide each by the total, 1 + 1/9 = 10/9, to get the weights.
Weight the readings and add them.
Read the result: 30.6 mm sits well below the midpoint of 33 mm, close to the steadier cue.

lead.text: Back to the first block. Sight reads 50 mm with an SD of 2 mm. Touch through the gloves reads 56 mm with an SD of 4 mm. Weight each cue by its reliability.

steps.headline: Two cues are sharper than one

lead.text: The combined estimate has a second advantage over each cue taken alone: it wobbles less. Two witnesses who each saw part of an event give a better account together than the better witness gives alone, because each fills in what the other left uncertain.

The SD of the combined estimate follows from the reliabilities. Add the two reliabilities and take the square root of the total. The combined SD is 1 divided by that root. Written out, it is 1 ÷ √(1/SD₁² + 1/SD₂²). Take two cues with SDs of 5 mm and 12 mm. Their reliabilities are 1/25 and 1/144, which add up to 169/3600. The square root of that is 13/60, and 1 divided by 13/60 is 60/13, about 4.6 mm. That is smaller than both 5 and 12.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the narrow teal curve is the combined estimate. It is taller and thinner than either cue's own curve, so using both senses pins the height down more tightly than the better sense could by itself. Even a poor cue helps, as long as its errors are unrelated to the other cue's errors.

lead.text: Two cues give independent readings of the same block. One has an SD of 3 mm and the other an SD of 4 mm. Use the formula for the combined SD.

steps.headline: What you expect is evidence too

lead.text: So far every cue has come through a sense. A third source of evidence needs no sense at all: what you already expect to see. Suppose a line flashes up for an instant and you cannot make out its tilt. If you expect it to be upright, that expectation pulls what you see towards upright.

The mind treats the expectation like one more cue. It has a reading, such as a tilt of 0° for an upright line, and an SD that says how firmly the expectation is held. Expectations built over many years are firm, so their SD is small and they carry a large weight whenever the glimpse is poor. An expectation used this way is called a prior, because it is in place before the new evidence arrives. Perception shaped by what you know and expect, instead of being built only from the incoming signal, is top-down processing.
In the figure, a line is expected to be upright (0°, SD 2°) and the glimpse says 8° (SD 4°).

afterFigure.text: The combined tilt stays close to upright. A hollow mask seen from the inside shows the same thing at a larger scale. Its surface is dented inwards, yet it looks like an ordinary face bulging outwards, because the expectation that faces bulge is so firm that it outweighs the shading that says otherwise.

lead.text: A line flashes up briefly. You expect it to be upright. Your eyes catch it only for an instant and report a tilt.

This is the ordinary state of perception. Neither sense hands you the block's true height. Each gives a report with some wobble in it, and the mind has to decide how far to believe each one before it settles on a single answer.

This lesson follows that one block. It begins with how a single sense gives a wobbly reading, adds a second sense and works out how much to trust each, and shows that two readings together are sharper than either. It ends with what you expect to see, which turns out to count as evidence as well.

lessons.title: Holding it in mind

steps.headline: Holding things in mind for a few seconds

lead.text: While you waited those ten seconds, something kept the digits available. Psychologists call it working memory: the small mental workspace that holds a few pieces of information for a short time while you use them. It is what lets you keep a phone number in mind while you walk across the room to dial it, or hold the start of a sentence while the end of it arrives.

Working memory differs from long-term memory, which holds your knowledge for years and has room for an enormous amount. Working memory is small and easily overwritten. If someone asks you a question before you reach the keypad, the number is often gone.

The size of the store was first estimated in 1956, when the psychologist George Miller gathered results from many experiments and concluded that people can hold about seven items at once, give or take two. That became one of the best-known numbers in psychology, yet it leaves the two lists unexplained. If the limit were seven items, list B would break it as badly as list A does. Something else must set the limit.

The answer turns on what an item is. Later work, notably by the psychologist Nelson Cowan in 2001, looked at what people can hold when they have no chance to repeat the items to themselves or to group them. The limit came out at about four, and the unit being counted is the chunk.

A chunk is a unit you already know as one thing. Someone who has never met the letters R, A and F together sees three separate letters, which make three chunks. A British reader knows RAF as the air force, so for that reader the same letters make a single chunk. The amount of memory used depends on what you know.

Now return to the two lists. List B runs 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9, a run you know so well that it behaves as one chunk. List A follows no pattern you know, so each digit is a chunk of its own. Nine chunks is more than the store can hold. The figure shows the same idea with an eleven-digit phone number.

afterFigure.text: Read as eleven separate digits, the number is far over the limit. Read as groups of five, three and three, it makes three chunks and fits with room to spare. The capacity is the same in both pictures. Only the number of chunks needed has changed.

lead.text: Nine unrelated digits are read once, with no way to group them. Each digit is its own chunk, and the capacity is four chunks.

If the limit is on chunks, and a chunk is whatever you know as one unit, there is a way to fit more into the same space: make each chunk carry more. This is chunking, the grouping of items into units you already know. A reader who knows the acronyms CD and TV sees the four letters CDTV as two chunks. Scramble them into DCVT and each letter becomes a chunk of its own, four in all.

The limit of about four chunks is the same for everyone. What differs is how much each chunk contains. Four single-letter chunks hold four letters. Four chunks that are each a three-letter acronym hold twelve.
Card numbers and postcodes are written in groups for this reason. The groups split a long string into pieces small enough to carry, and people who learn the groups well can carry them without effort.
Chunks depend on what the reader already knows. Count the pieces this reader would hold.

steps.headline: How a chess master remembers a board

lead.text: Chunking is easiest to see in experts. In the early 1970s William Chase and Herbert Simon showed a chess master and some weaker players a real game position for five seconds, then asked each of them to rebuild it from memory. The master put back far more of the pieces.

It would be easy to guess that masters simply have better memories. A second condition says otherwise. When the pieces were placed at random, as they never would be in a game, the master's advantage mostly disappeared. A master has seen so many real positions that a cluster of pieces, such as a castled king with the three pawns in front of it, is one familiar pattern. A weaker player sees the same cluster as separate pieces. With random placements the patterns are gone, and the master has nothing to chunk.
So the master's working memory is ordinary, with the same limit of about four chunks. The difference lies in how much each chunk holds. The figure shows a simplified position of twelve pieces.

afterFigure.text: The master sees the twelve pieces as three patterns, which fit in a store of four chunks. The novice sees twelve single pieces, which overflow it.

lead.text: Now take a larger, real position of 20 pieces. The master recalls all of it, grouped into 4 chunks.

So far working memory has been a single store with a size. In 1974 the psychologists Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch argued that it is better described as a small team of parts, each handling a different kind of material, with a controller above them. The model has been revised since, but its main parts have held up.

The phonological loop holds sounds and words. It is the voice in your head that repeats a phone number to keep it alive. The visuospatial sketchpad holds images and positions, such as the layout of a room or the route you are about to walk. The episodic buffer ties material from these parts and from long-term memory into one scene or story. Above them sits the central executive, which stores nothing itself. It directs attention and decides what to hold and what to drop.

Separate parts explain something a single store cannot. Two jobs that use different parts, such as remembering a phone number and picturing a route, interfere with each other very little. Two jobs that use the same part, such as holding two phone numbers at once, interfere a great deal.
Each part of the model has its own job, and one of them does not hold material at all.
People recalled short lists of words in the order they heard them. Some lists sounded alike, such as man, cat, map. Others did not, such as pit, day, cow.

Most people find list B easy and list A a struggle, with the early digits slipping away by the fifth or sixth. Yet both lists are nine digits long, and they contain exactly the same digits. They take the same time to read. The length cannot be what makes B easier.

This lesson tries to find out what it is. It starts with the short-term workspace that held those digits for ten seconds, and the limit on what fits in it. It then shows how knowledge stretches that limit, using a chess master as the best example, and ends by looking at how the workspace is organised inside.

lessons.title: Forgetting and spaced retrieval

lead.text: Return to the 100 words. You lost 40 in the first day, and the 60 that remain are the ones that stuck best, so they go more slowly. Say 10 more go over the following week and a few more over the month after. Draw a graph of how much you can recall against the time since you learned the words, and the result is a curve that falls steeply at first and then flattens.

Hermann Ebbinghaus found this shape in the 1880s. He learned lists of nonsense syllables and tested himself after different delays. In 2015 Jaap Murre and Joeri Dros repeated the experiment with one volunteer and got a curve of the same shape, so the pattern has held up for well over a century.

The curve describes memory in general, and it does not fit every memory equally well. Some memories are strong and fall along a flat curve. Others are fragile and drop quickly. To make use of the curve we need a number that says which kind of memory we have.

steps.headline: A number for how long a memory lasts

lead.text: The number is called stability, written S. It is the number of days until the chance of recalling the memory has fallen to 90%. A memory with a stability of 3 days is still 90% likely to come back after 3 days. A memory with a stability of 30 days takes ten times as long to reach that point.

With S in hand, one formula gives the predicted recall R after t days: R = 1 ÷ (1 + t ÷ 9S). Here 9S means 9 × S. At t = 0 the fraction is zero and R = 1 ÷ 1 = 100%. As t grows the fraction grows and R falls, steeply at first and then more slowly, which is the curve Ebbinghaus found. Put t = S and the fraction is 1/9, so R = 1 ÷ (1 + 1/9) = 0.9, which matches the definition of S.

Take S = 3 days and look at day 18. Then 9S = 27 and t ÷ 9S = 18 ÷ 27 = 2/3. That gives R = 1 ÷ (1 + 2/3) = 3/5, which is 60%. The figure draws the whole curve for a memory with a stability of 3 days.

afterFigure.text: Press play and watch recall fall. Stability sits under the fraction, so a larger S makes t ÷ 9S grow more slowly and the curve flatter. A memory with a large stability fades slowly, and one with a small stability fades fast.

lead.text: A memory has a stability of S = 10 days. Use the curve R = 1 ÷ (1 + t ÷ 9S).

steps.headline: What a review does to a memory

lead.text: So far the memory has been left alone. Now suppose you test yourself on the words on day 4 and recall them correctly. A successful recall does two things. It lifts recall back to nearly 100%, as if the clock had restarted, and it raises the memory's stability, so the curve that follows is flatter than the one before.

Each success multiplies the stability by some factor. If a review multiplies it by 2.5, a memory with S = 2 days becomes one with S = 5 days, and forgetting from then on is two and a half times as slow. This is why reviews can be spaced further and further apart. The second review can wait longer than the first, and the third longer still.

Reviewing at widening gaps is called spaced practice, also known as distributed practice. The opposite is massed practice, which crams all the study into one session. The figure compares a memory reviewed on day 3 with one that is left alone.

afterFigure.text: The reviewed memory is back near 100% on day 3 and then declines far more slowly than the other. By the end of the month the gap between them is large, even though the reviewed memory cost only one short test.

Divide t by 9S.
Put it in the curve.
Read it as a percentage: 75%.

lead.text: A memory starts with a stability of 2 days. A review on day 4 triples it, from 2 days to 6 days. Now measure from that review.

steps.headline: Choosing the day of the next review

lead.text: A review that comes too early wastes effort, because the memory is still strong. One that comes too late finds it already faded. A good schedule picks the day when predicted recall has just fallen to a target, and a common target is 90%. Discere schedules reviews this way with FSRS, a scheduling model built on a forgetting curve like the one above.
Stability was defined as the days until recall falls to 90%, so a card with stability S is due S days after its last review. The 90% target needs no further calculation.

Success then multiplies S and the next gap grows. Take a card with S = 2 days, and suppose each success multiplies stability by 2.5. It is due after 2 days. Its stability then becomes 5, so the next review is due 5 days later, on day 7. Stability becomes 12.5 and the gap after that is 12.5 days. The gaps are 2, 5 and 12.5 days, each longer than the last.

afterFigure.text: Each dot in the figure is a review. After each one recall returns to nearly 100%, and each curve that follows is flatter, so the dots sit further and further apart. That widening is the pattern to expect from any spaced schedule.

lead.text: Reviews are scheduled for the moment that predicted recall falls to the 90% target.

There is one more choice to make about a review, which is how to do it. You can reread your notes, which feels smooth and familiar. Or you can close them and try to recall what they said, which feels harder and more uncertain. The second method is called retrieval practice, and it is the kind of review the stability story assumed, since a review there means a successful act of recall.

Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke compared the two in 2006. Students studied a passage and then either reread it or practised recalling it. Five minutes later the rereaders did better, recalling 81% of the ideas in the passage against 75%. If the test had stopped there, rereading would have looked like the better method.

The students were tested again a week later and the order reversed. Those who had practised recalling kept far more than those who had reread. Effortful recall feels worse at the time and lasts longer, so the feeling that rereading is going well is a poor guide to what will last. This is why good flashcard systems make you try to answer before they show you the card.
A week after studying, students who had practised recall were compared with students who had reread. The counts are in the picture.

The question is what happens over the following weeks. A natural guess is that you keep losing words at the same pace, another 40 the next day and nothing left by the third. Most people's experience says otherwise, since whatever survives the first day tends to last much longer. Memory fades along a curve with a definite shape, and that shape can be written down.

lessons.title: Conditioning and reinforcement

lead.text: In the 1890s the Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov was studying digestion in dogs when he noticed that they began to drool before any food reached them, at the sight of the person who usually brought it. He turned that observation into an experiment. Food makes a hungry dog drool without any training, and a bell makes it prick up its ears and do little else.

Pavlov rang the bell just before the food arrived, again and again. After enough of these pairings the dog drooled at the bell alone. The bell had become a conditioned stimulus, a signal that has gained its power through experience, and drooling at it was learned. Learning in which a signal comes to predict an outcome through repeated pairing is called classical conditioning.

The pairing matters. A bell that rings at random times, with no link to the food, teaches the dog nothing, because the bell tells it nothing about what comes next. That leaves a question about pace. The first pairing is the biggest surprise to the dog and later ones surprise it less, and a simple rule describes how the learning grows.

In 1972 Robert Rescorla and Allan Wagner proposed that rule. Call the strength of the link between bell and food V, the associative strength. It starts at 0 and can rise towards a maximum, written λ (the Greek letter lambda), which is the most the food can support. With food present, λ = 1.

Each pairing closes a share of the gap between V and λ. The rule is ΔV = rate × (λ − V), where ΔV is the change in V on that trial and the rate says how quickly the animal learns, a number between 0 and 1. Take a rate of 0.25. On the first pairing V is 0, so the gap is 1 and V rises by 0.25 × 1 = 0.25. On the second pairing the gap is 1 − 0.25 = 0.75, so V rises by 0.25 × 0.75 = 0.1875 and reaches 0.4375. The figure shows six pairings.

afterFigure.text: Each step is smaller than the one before, because less of the gap is left to close. The first pairing teaches the most and the tenth teaches very little. That fits the dog that is quick to start drooling and then settles into a steady response.

lead.text: A bell is paired with food twice. The rate is 0.3, the maximum is 1, and V starts at 0.

Suppose the bell keeps ringing after the food has been taken away. The same rule applies, with one change. With no food the most the bell can predict is 0, so λ = 0. If V stands at 0.8 and the rate is 0.25, the gap λ − V is −0.8, which is negative, so V moves down by 0.25 × 0.8 = 0.2 to 0.6. A bell that no longer predicts food loses its power, trial by trial. This fading response is called extinction.

Extinction does not wipe the dog's learning clean. If the bell is rung again after a rest, the drooling often returns for a while, which is called spontaneous recovery. It looks as though extinction adds a second piece of learning, that the bell no longer means food, on top of the first and leaves the first in place. The simple rule treats extinction as unlearning, so it is a good first model and an incomplete one.

The dog has so far learned from what comes before an event: the bell. Now ask what happens to an action that is followed by something. Teach the dog to sit by giving it a treat each time it sits, and it sits more often. Sitting was followed by a consequence, and the consequence changed how likely the behaviour is. This is operant conditioning, studied by B. F. Skinner and, before him, by Edward Thorndike.

Two choices describe any consequence. It either adds something or takes something away, and psychologists call these positive and negative, words that only mean added and removed. It also either makes the behaviour more likely, which is reinforcement, or less likely, which is punishment.

The treat for sitting adds something pleasant and sitting rises, so it is positive reinforcement. A car's seat-belt alarm stops once the belt is fastened, so removing an unpleasant sound makes fastening more likely, which is negative reinforcement. A library fine takes money away and late returns fall, which is negative punishment. Touching a hot hob adds pain and the touching falls, which is positive punishment.
Decide whether something was added or removed, and whether the behaviour rose or fell.

A trainer must also decide how often to give the treat. The rule for when a reward is given is a schedule of reinforcement. Some schedules depend on how many responses the animal makes, and some depend on how much time has passed.

A fixed-ratio schedule gives a reward after a set number of responses, such as every fourth peck. Under a variable-ratio schedule the number changes unpredictably around an average, so the reward might follow 2 pecks, then 7, then 3. A fixed-interval schedule rewards the first response after a set time has passed, so the reward lands on a response and responses during the wait earn nothing. A variable-interval schedule makes the wait unpredictable. The figure records responses over time for a fixed ratio of 4 and a variable ratio that averages 4.

afterFigure.text: The two pay out about equally often, but they differ in what happens when the rewards stop. On a fixed schedule the animal soon sees that the pattern has broken and gives up. On a variable-ratio schedule it cannot tell a long gap from the end of the rewards, so it keeps responding for far longer. An angler whose fish bite after an unpredictable number of casts knows the effect.

lessons.title: Base rates and Bayes

lead.text: Go back to the airport and count. Among the 1,000 bags, 2 hold a banned item and the scanner beeps for both. Of the other 998 it beeps for 98. In total the scanner beeps for 2 + 98 = 100 bags. A bag that has beeped is one of those 100, and only 2 of them hold anything banned. A beep means a banned item about 2 times in 100.

That answer came from counting bags. No percentages had to be multiplied. Picturing a crowd of real things and counting them is a method known as natural frequencies, and it makes problems of this kind much easier. Percentages describe a group but hide the individuals in it. Once a percentage is turned into a number of people, the arithmetic is only counting.

Here is the move in general. Suppose 2% of a group of 1,000 people have a condition. Two per cent of 1,000 is 20 people. If a test catches half of them, that is 10 people. Each step takes a percentage of a group and turns it into a head count, and the next step works from that count.

Now take a medical screening test. The condition is present in 2% of 1,000 people, and the share of a group who have a condition is called the base rate, here 2%. The test is imperfect. It flags half of the people who have the condition, which is its hit rate, and it also flags 5% of the people who do not, its false-alarm rate.

Counting gives the whole picture. Two per cent of 1,000 is 20 people with the condition, and half of them, 10 people, are flagged. These are the true positives: people with the condition whom the test flags. The other 980 people are healthy, and 5% of 980 is 49 people flagged by mistake. These are the false positives: healthy people whom the test flags. The figure draws the 1,000 people in this way.

afterFigure.text: The false positives outnumber the true positives by almost five to one, although the test catches half of the people who have the condition and wrongly flags only one healthy person in twenty. The healthy group is so much larger than the group with the condition that even a small error rate produces many flags.

lead.text: 1,000 people are screened for a disease that 1% have. The test flags 90% of those who have it, so there are 9 true positives. It also wrongly flags 10% of people who do not have the disease.

Most people, shown a result like this, answer with the test's hit rate. A test that catches 90% of cases seems to mean that a positive result is 90% likely to be right. The accuracy of the test is vivid and the rarity of the condition is easy to overlook, so the vivid number wins. Ignoring how common something is when judging a single case is called base-rate neglect.

The mistake shows up outside medicine too. Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described a man called Steve, who is shy and tidy and loves order. They asked people whether he is more likely to be a librarian or a farmer. People chose librarian because the description sounds like one. But farmers vastly outnumber librarians, and that fact is evidence as well. People let the description crowd it out.
The next screen gives a way to avoid the mistake. It puts both numbers, how rare the condition is and how good the test is, into a single count.

steps.headline: Who the positive result is about

lead.text: A person who has just tested positive belongs to one particular group, the people the test flagged. That group is made up of the true positives and the false positives together. The chance that this person has the condition is the share of the flagged group who really do.

The calculation is true positives ÷ (true positives + false positives). Go back to the 1,000 people screened with a base rate of 2%. There were 10 true positives and 49 false positives. That makes 59 flagged people, and 10 ÷ 59 is about 0.17. A positive result there gives about a 17% chance of having the condition, far below the 50% that the hit rate might suggest.

Dividing by the 20 people who have the condition would answer a different question, which is how likely a person with the condition is to be flagged. That is the hit rate again. A positive result is a fact about the flagged group, so the flagged group is the number to divide by.

lead.text: The test was never the whole problem. Its hit rate and false-alarm rate describe how it behaves on people who have the condition and on people who do not. What a positive result means also depends on the mix of people being tested. Move the same test into a clinic where patients have been sent because of symptoms, and the mix changes.

Suppose 20% of the 1,000 people tested at the clinic have the condition, and the test is as before: it flags half of them and 5% of the healthy. Now 200 people have the condition and 100 of them are flagged. Of the 800 healthy people, 40 are flagged. The flagged group holds 140 people and 100 of them have the condition, which is about 71%. Compare that with 17% when only 2% were affected. The figure sets the two crowds side by side.

Most people's first reaction is that the scanner is very good. It caught both of the bags that mattered and was wrong about fewer than one in ten of the others, so a beep must mean trouble. lessons.title: Anchors and fast thinking

lead.text: Go back to the jacket. The “was £200” label works as an anchor, a number you meet before you make a judgement, which then pulls the judgement towards itself. Nobody claims £200 is the jacket's real value. It only has to be in front of you when you decide what £120 means.

People have tested this with numbers that were plainly meaningless. Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, two psychologists who spent decades studying how people judge, built a wheel of fortune rigged to stop at either 10 or 65. Volunteers watched it stop, then answered a question with nothing to do with the wheel. They were asked what percentage of the member countries of the United Nations are in Africa.

Each volunteer gave one guess. To compare two groups, line up each group's guesses from lowest to highest and take the one in the middle, the median. A few wild answers cannot drag it far, so it shows the typical guess. A pull from a number that carries no information is called anchoring bias. A gap between two percentages is counted in percentage points.
The wheel stopped at 10 for one group and at 65 for the other. The median guess was 25% after the 10 and 45% after the 65.

lead.text: A gap between the groups shows an anchor at work, but a single gap cannot be compared with other studies. Studies use different anchors, and a gap of 20 means something different when the anchors were 10 apart than when they were 100 apart. What counts is how much of the distance between the anchors turns up in the guesses.

The anchoring index measures that. Take the gap between the two median guesses and divide it by the gap between the two anchors. An index of 0 means the anchors did nothing, because both groups guessed alike. An index of 1 means the guesses moved as far as the anchors, so people simply repeated the number they were shown. Anchors of 0 and 100 with medians of 30 and 50 give 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2.

lead.text: An anchor is a number someone puts in front of you. Judgement gets a second push from your own memory. Asked how common something is, you rarely count. You check how easily examples come to mind and treat an easy flood of them as a sign that the thing is common.

That shortcut is a heuristic, a rule of thumb that gives a decent answer with little effort. This one is the availability heuristic: judging how common something is by how easily examples come to mind. It works when memorable things really are frequent. It fails when something sticks in memory for another reason. Plane crashes fill the news and car crashes rarely do, so many people think flying is riskier than driving.

Here is a puzzle you can check. Compare English words that start with k with English words that have k as the third letter. Most people say the first kind is more common. Searching memory by a word's first letter is far easier than by its third, so words like “king” and “kettle” arrive at once while “ask” and “like” hardly come up. Words with k third are about twice as common.
A sample of 600 English words that contain k gives a way to check the guess most people make.

steps.headline: A quick answer and a slow check

lead.text: A third shortcut is the simplest: the first answer that pops into your head. Following Kahneman, psychologists call fast, effortless thinking System 1, and the slower, deliberate checking that can follow it System 2. These are names for two ways of thinking and do not match two organs in the brain. You move between them all day.

System 1 is usually right, which is why it is in charge. It lets you catch a ball or read a face without a calculation. The trouble comes with a problem that looks easy and is not, because System 1 hands over its answer so smoothly that nothing prompts a check. Try a small one. A cap and a scarf cost £6 together, and the scarf costs £4 more than the cap. The answer that springs to mind is that the cap costs £2. Put it back into the problem: a £2 cap makes the scarf £6, and the pair cost £8.

To solve it properly, call the cap's price x. The scarf is x + 4, so together they cost 2x + 4 = 6, which gives x = 1. The cap costs £1. The habit to keep is putting the quick answer back into the problem and seeing whether the total still works. It takes a few seconds, and it is worth doing when a wrong answer would be expensive.

The £200 told you nothing true about the jacket. It was simply the first number you saw, and your sense of what £120 means was measured from it. Quick judgement works like this a good deal of the time. What you meet first, and what comes to mind most easily, quietly shapes the answer you give.

lessons.title: Conformity, obedience and bystanders

steps.headline: Matching lines in a room of strangers

lead.text: The first set of experiments was run by Solomon Asch in the 1950s. A volunteer joined a small group for what was described as an eyesight test. Everyone looked at one line and at three comparison lines, and said aloud which comparison matched. The right answer was obvious, and people working alone got it wrong on fewer than one judgement in a hundred.

What the volunteer did not know was that everyone else was an actor working for the experimenter, called a confederate. On some rounds the confederates all gave the same wrong answer before the volunteer's turn. Those are the critical trials, and what the volunteer said on one is a critical answer. Giving the group's wrong answer when your own eyes say otherwise is conformity.

afterFigure.text: About 37 critical answers in every 100 followed the wrong majority, and about 75 people in every 100 went along at least once. To get a rate, divide the critical answers that conformed by all the critical answers. Ten people facing 8 critical trials each give 10 × 8 = 80 critical answers, and if 24 followed the majority the rate is 24 ÷ 80 = 30%.

model.setting: Asch's majority condition, about 37 in every 100 critical answers
Asch's majority condition, about 75 in every 100 people

lead.text: A replication of the line task used 18 people. Each gave 12 critical answers, and 72 of all those answers followed the wrong majority.

Asch showed that a group can change what people say. In 1961 Stanley Milgram, a psychologist at Yale, asked what happens when an authority simply tells someone to continue. Volunteers were told they were helping with a study of learning. As the teacher, each had to give a learner an electric shock for every wrong answer, raising the voltage with each mistake, up to a switch marked 450 volts.

The learner was an actor and the shocks were not real, though the volunteers believed they were. As the learner protested and then fell silent, many volunteers hesitated. An experimenter in a grey lab coat answered with calm instructions such as “Please continue.” Obedience is following the instructions of someone you accept as an authority, and Milgram measured it as the share of volunteers who went all the way to the 450-volt switch.
Before the study, people asked to predict the result expected very few to go that far. In the first version, with the learner in another room, most did.
In the first version, with the learner in another room, 26 of the 40 volunteers went on to the final 450-volt switch.

Milgram then moved the learner nearer to see whether distance mattered. At first the learner was in another room and could only be heard. Next he sat in the same room as the volunteer. Closest of all, the volunteer had to press the learner's hand onto a shock plate with their own.

afterFigure.text: Each step closer lowered obedience. In the same room, 16 of 40 went to the end, and with the hand on the plate, 12 of 40 did. To compare two conditions, turn each count into a percentage of its own group and subtract. The difference is in percentage points, so a rate that falls from 50% to 40% has fallen 10 percentage points. Closeness weakened obedience without removing it.

lead.text: The closest version had the volunteer press the learner's hand onto the plate. Compare it with the learner in another room.

steps.headline: How the results have held up

lead.text: Milgram's numbers have been checked, and the checks add detail. Modern ethics rules forbid running his study as it was. In 2009 Jerry Burger ran a version that stopped at 150 volts, the point beyond which most of Milgram's volunteers had gone on to the end. Burger found 70% willing to continue past 150 volts, against 82.5% in Milgram's comparable condition.

A gap that small leaves the main finding standing. Another line of work asks how far the original percentages can be trusted. Gina Perry, an author who went through Milgram's archives, found that experimenters sometimes left the script and pushed volunteers harder than planned, and that many volunteers doubted the shocks were real. A volunteer who suspects the shocks are fake tells you less about obedience.

The careful reading is that obedience to authority is real and weakens with closeness. The exact percentages depend on the setting and on what volunteers believed was happening, so a figure like 65% belongs to one setting and should be quoted with it.

steps.headline: Why a crowd can mean less help

lead.text: Back on the platform, a crowd has two effects that pull in opposite directions. More people means more chances that somebody helps. It can also make each person less likely to help, because everyone can see that others could act and responsibility feels shared out. Psychologists call that diffusion of responsibility.

John Darley and Bibb Latané tested it in 1968. Volunteers joined an intercom discussion, each alone in a separate room. One speaker seemed to have a seizure. Volunteers who believed they were the only listener helped 85% of the time. Volunteers who believed four others were listening helped 31% of the time. Every volunteer was alone in a room, so the difference came from what they believed about the other listeners.
Those percentages are chances for one person. Whether anyone helps depends on how the individual chances add up across the group, and the next screen works that out.

Suppose each person in a crowd decides independently, which means one person's choice does not change another's. The chance that at least one of them acts is easiest to find through the opposite event, that nobody acts. If each of three people acts with probability 0.3, each fails to act with probability 0.7.

Nobody acts only if all three fail, and for independent people you multiply their chances: 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7 = 0.343. So the chance that at least one acts is 1 − 0.343 = 0.657, or 65.7%. For n people who each act with probability p, the rule is 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ.

afterFigure.text: A lone witness with probability 0.85 beats three witnesses at 0.3 each, whose group chance is 65.7%. A larger crowd gives more chances, but the group does better only if each person's own chance does not fall too far.

lead.text: Two people watch the same emergency. Each decides alone, and each has a one in two chance of acting.

steps.headline: What cameras saw in real streets

lead.text: Laboratory results like these fed a famous story. In 1964 a woman named Kitty Genovese was killed in New York, and a newspaper reported that 38 neighbours watched and did nothing. The story was used for decades to illustrate the bystander effect. The figure of 38 silent witnesses has since been shown to be largely a myth, and some neighbours did call the police.

A better test is to count what happens in real conflicts. Richard Philpot and colleagues studied CCTV recordings of 219 real street conflicts in three cities. In 91% of them at least one bystander stepped in, and the more people were present the more likely it was that someone did.

That fits the arithmetic of the last screen. Even when each person has only a small chance of acting, several people together make it likely that somebody does. What survives from the laboratory is a claim about the individual, who is somewhat less likely to act when others are present. The old story that a crowd means nobody helps does not survive.
Five bystanders watch a street conflict. Each decides independently, and each acts with probability 0.2.
