blocks.text: On an empty station platform, a stranger collapses in front of you. You are the only person who has seen it, so helping is up to you. On a crowded platform the same stranger collapses in front of forty people, and each of them sees exactly what you would have seen.

It seems obvious that more onlookers means more help. The research is less comfortable, and the same is true of much that other people do to us. Their opinions can change what we say we see. An authority's instruction can lead ordinary people to do things they would refuse alone. A crowd can leave each member feeling that helping is somebody else's job.

This lesson goes through three classic sets of experiments on that influence. Each one gives a number you can calculate, either a percentage of people or a probability. All three have since been checked and criticised. You'll learn to read the numbers and the criticism together.

questions.onCorrect: When the arrow runs from mood to exercise, being in a good mood leads to more exercise. The correlation alone cannot rule it out.

misconceptions.feedback: That has the arrow running from exercise to mood, the direction the data seem to suggest.
That puts a third variable behind both measures. No arrow runs between exercise and mood.

questions.prompt: 6 of 20 full-moon shifts were busy, and 30 of 100 other shifts were busy. By how many percentage points does the busy rate differ between the two kinds of shift?
hints: Turn each count into a rate before comparing.
Divide busy shifts by all shifts in each group.
Subtract one rate from the other.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6/20 = 30% and 30/100 = 30%, so the difference is 0 percentage points. The remembered link is an illusory correlation.

questions.onCorrect: Both groups were busy at the same rate. The vivid full-moon nights were memorable, not more frequent.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts raw counts, but the groups differ in size. Turn each into a rate first.
That compares the quiet shifts, which are different in number. Compare rates, not counts.

questions.prompt: Daily screen time and sleep quality correlate at r = −0.3. What percentage of the variation in sleep quality is shared with screen time?
hints: Use the square of the correlation coefficient.
The minus sign disappears when you square.
Square 0.3 and convert to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: r² = 0.3² = 0.09, so 9%. A modest correlation leaves 91% of the variation to other causes.

questions.onCorrect: Square r and the sign drops out. A modest correlation shares only a small slice of the variation.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads r as a percentage. Square it first.
That is the share left over, not the share they have in common.

questions.prompt: A researcher records 'aggression' as the number of seconds a participant holds down a button that blasts noise at an opponent. What do we call a definition that turns a concept into a precise measurement like this?
hints: The definition tells you the operation used to measure the concept.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is an operational definition: it states exactly how aggression will be measured.

questions.onCorrect: An operational definition says exactly how a concept is measured, so anyone could repeat the measurement.

misconceptions.feedback: Those name the variable set and the variable measured. This asks what turns a concept into a measurement.

questions.prompt: Four members who choose the programme exercise 9, 8, 8 and 7 hours a week. The other four exercise 3, 2, 2 and 1. How many hours a week higher is the programme group's average, before the programme starts?
hints: Find each group's mean separately.
Add the four values in a group and divide by four.
Subtract the comparison group's mean from the programme group's mean.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Programme mean = (9 + 8 + 8 + 7)/4 = 8; other mean = (3 + 2 + 2 + 1)/4 = 2; the head start is 6 hours.

questions.onCorrect: Each group's average is its total divided by four. The joiners' head start is built in by choice.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the programme group's own average. The question asks how far ahead it is of the other group.
That compares totals, and both groups have four people. Compare the averages instead.

questions.prompt: Random assignment gives every participant an equal what of being placed in each condition? Answer in one word.
hints: Think of a coin toss deciding each person's group.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An equal chance: assignment depends on the draw, never on the person.

questions.onCorrect: Assignment depends on the draw, never on the person, so no trait can decide who gets the programme.

misconceptions.feedback: Choosing is self-selection. Random assignment takes the choice away.

questions.prompt: Is resting heart rate the independent or the dependent variable?
hints: Ask which variable the researchers set and which they measure.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Resting heart rate is the dependent variable: it is measured to see the programme's effect.

questions.onCorrect: Resting heart rate is measured afterwards to see the programme's effect, so it depends on the condition.

misconceptions.feedback: The independent variable is the one the researchers set. Resting heart rate is measured after the condition is set.

questions.prompt: In a drug trial the drug group improves by 12 points and the placebo group by 8 points. How many points of improvement can be attributed to the drug's active ingredient?
hints: The placebo group improves without any active ingredient.
Remove the improvement that both groups share.
Subtract the placebo improvement from the drug improvement.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 − 8 = 4 points. The placebo group shows how much improvement expectation and time alone produce.

questions.onCorrect: Remove what both groups share. The placebo group shows what expectation and time produce alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the drug group's whole improvement, including what expectation alone produces.
That is the improvement without the active ingredient. Ask what the drug added beyond it.
Adding the groups mixes the two responses together. You need what is left after removing the shared part.

questions.prompt: A random draw puts people with prior fitness scores 4, 6, 5 and 7 in the treatment group, and 6, 5, 4 and 5 in the control group. What is the treatment mean minus the control mean?
hints: Find the mean of each group of four.
The treatment scores add to 22.
Subtract the control mean from the treatment mean.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Treatment mean = 22/4 = 5.5; control mean = 20/4 = 5; the chance gap is 0.5.

questions.onCorrect: Each mean is its total divided by four. The chance gap is small, as random assignment leads you to expect.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the treatment group's own mean. Subtract the control group's mean from it.
Check the order. The question asks for the treatment mean minus the control mean.

questions.prompt: In a trial, neither the participants nor the researchers who measure them know who received the real treatment. What is this design called?
hints: Count how many parties are kept unaware.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is a double-blind design: both sides are kept unaware of the conditions.

questions.onCorrect: Both sides are kept unaware of the conditions, so neither expectation nor measuring can lean toward the treatment.

misconceptions.feedback: A single-blind design keeps only one party unaware. Count how many parties are unaware here.

questions.prompt: A control group scores 100 on average and a training group 106, with a standard deviation of 15 in both. What is Cohen's d?
hints: Cohen's d is a difference measured in standard deviations.
Find the difference between the two means.
Divide that difference by 15.
questions.onCorrect: d is the difference between means measured in standard deviations: a gain of 6 beside a spread of 15.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the raw difference. Cohen's d measures it against the spread.
That divides the spread by the difference. d divides the difference by the spread.

questions.prompt: Two equal-sized groups have means 40 and 46.5 with standard deviations 7 and 17. Using the pooled SD √[(SD₁² + SD₂²)/2], what is Cohen's d?
hints: Square each standard deviation before averaging.
Average 49 and 289, then take the square root.
Divide the 6.5-point difference by the pooled SD.
questions.onCorrect: Pool the spreads from their squares, then divide the difference by that pooled SD.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the plain average of the two SDs. Pool the spreads through their squares.
That is the raw difference. Divide it by the pooled spread.

questions.prompt: A team studies an effect of d = 0.4 and wants 80% power at α = 0.05. By Lehr's rule of thumb, how many participants per group do they need?
hints: Square the effect size first.
0.4 squared is 0.16.
Divide 16 by the squared effect size.
questions.onCorrect: The need grows with 1 ÷ d²: for this effect, 16 divided by the square of d.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by d. The rule divides by d squared.
That is the top of the fraction. Divide it by d squared.

questions.prompt: A replication finds means of 50.4 (depleted) and 50.0 (control), both with standard deviation 10. What is Cohen's d?
hints: Divide the difference between means by the standard deviation.
The difference between the means is under one point.
Divide 0.4 by 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: d = (50.4 − 50.0)/10 = 0.04, close to zero and far below the published average of about 0.6.

questions.onCorrect: The means differ by well under a tenth of a standard deviation, so the published effect did not hold.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the raw difference in points. Divide it by the standard deviation.
That divides the SD by the difference. d divides the difference by the SD.

questions.prompt: Of 97 original studies with significant results, 35 replications were significant. What percentage replicated? Give one decimal place.
hints: Divide the successful replications by the studies attempted.
Use 97 as the denominator, since only significant originals count.
Convert 35/97 to a percentage and round to one decimal place.
questions.onCorrect: Only the 97 significant originals count. The replications that succeeded, over that base, give about a third.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count of studies that replicated. The question asks for a percentage.
That is the share that did not replicate. The question asks for the share that did.

questions.prompt: Which claim failed a large preregistered replication and should be treated as a cautionary case, not established fact?
hints: Two of the options are definitions or arithmetic; one is an empirical claim.

acceptedIdeas: Holding a power pose for two minutes raises testosterone
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ranehill and colleagues (2015) found no hormonal effect of power poses in 200 people. The other two statements are mathematical facts.

choices.label: Holding a power pose for two minutes raises testosterone
Random assignment balances groups on average
Squaring r gives the shared variance

questions.onCorrect: Power posing's hormone effect failed a large replication. Arithmetic facts and balancing by chance are not claims that can fail that way.

misconceptions.feedback: Random assignment balancing groups on average is a property of chance, not a finding that was overturned.
Squaring r is arithmetic, so it cannot fail a replication.

questions.prompt: What is the hit rate as a percentage?
hints: A hit is a yes on a trial where the signal is present.
Divide by the number of scans with a tumour, not all scans.
Convert 40/50 to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: The hit rate is hits divided by signal trials, so only scans with a tumour count in the denominator.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of hits. Turn it into a share of the scans that had a tumour.
That is the share of tumour scans she missed. The hit rate is the share she caught.
That is the rate as a decimal. The question asks for a percentage.

questions.prompt: A guard has a hit rate of 0.80 (z = 0.84) and a false-alarm rate of 0.20 (z = −0.84). What is d′?
hints: d′ subtracts the false-alarm z-score from the hit z-score.
Subtracting a negative number adds its size.
Calculate 0.84 + 0.84.
questions.onCorrect: d′ = z(H) − z(FA), and subtracting a negative z-score adds its size.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats both z-scores as having the same sign. The false-alarm z-score is negative.
That is only one of the two z-scores. d′ combines both.

questions.prompt: Another guard shouts readily at the same car park. Her hit rate is 0.954 (z = 1.68) and her false-alarm rate is 0.50 (z = 0). What is her d′?
hints: Use the same formula as before with the new z-scores.
The z-score of a 0.50 rate is zero.
Subtract the false-alarm z-score from the hit z-score.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: d′ = 1.68 − 0 = 1.68. Sensitivity is unchanged; only the criterion moved.

questions.onCorrect: Moving the criterion changed both rates but not the curves, so d′ stays the same.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the larger z-score from itself. Use z(H) − z(FA) with these values.
That halves the difference. d′ is the difference itself.

questions.prompt: A baggage screener has z(H) = 1.68 and z(FA) = 0. What is her criterion location c = −[z(H) + z(FA)]/2?
hints: Add the two z-scores first.
Halve the sum.
Keep the minus sign in front of the bracket.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: c = −(1.68 + 0)/2 = −0.84. A negative c means a bias towards saying yes.

questions.onCorrect: A negative c means a bias towards yes. Halve the sum of the z-scores and keep the minus sign.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign. A screener who leans towards yes has a c below zero.
That leaves out the halving. Divide the sum by two.

questions.prompt: A lifeguard spots swimmers in difficulty with hit rate 0.69 (z = 0.50) and raises false alarms at rate 0.07 (z = −1.48). What is d′?
hints: Subtract z(FA) from z(H).
The false-alarm z-score is negative.
Add 0.50 and 1.48.
questions.onCorrect: Subtract z(FA) from z(H). The false-alarm z-score is negative, so d′ is the sum of their sizes.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the sizes. The false-alarm z-score is negative, so subtracting it adds.
That is only the false-alarm z-score's size. d′ also uses the hit z-score.

questions.prompt: Lowering the criterion so an observer says yes more often increases hits. Which other outcome, on trials with no signal, does it also increase?
hints: Think about the yes responses on trials with no signal.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It also increases false alarms: more yes responses when no signal is present.

questions.onCorrect: A lower criterion means more yes answers everywhere, including false alarms on noise trials.

misconceptions.feedback: Lowering the criterion reduces misses. Think about trials with no signal at all.
More yes answers means fewer correct rejections, not more.

questions.prompt: In a class demonstration, 14 of the 30 people counting basketball passes failed to notice the gorilla. What percentage missed it? Give one decimal place.
hints: Divide the number who missed it by the number watching.
The denominator is 30.
Convert 14/30 to a percentage and round to one decimal place.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 14/30 = 0.4667, or 46.7%, close to the 46% Simons and Chabris reported.

questions.onCorrect: Divide those who missed it by all who watched: nearly half failed to notice something in plain view.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of people who missed it. Turn it into a percentage of everyone watching.
That is the share who noticed it. The question asks for the share who missed it.

questions.prompt: Each trial takes 600 ms and each change of task adds 200 ms. How long does the sequence ABABABAB take in total, in milliseconds?
hints: Count the places where the letter changes.
Every trial costs 600 ms; each switch adds 200 ms.
Add 8 × 600 to the number of switches × 200.
questions.onCorrect: Trial time plus switch time: eight trials, and a switch before every trial except the first.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the trials. Each change of task adds more.
Eight trials make only seven changes. Count the gaps where the task changes.

questions.prompt: Each trial takes 600 ms and each change of task adds 200 ms. How many milliseconds longer does ABABABAB take than AAAABBBB?
hints: Both sequences have eight trials, so only switches differ.
Count the switches in each sequence.
Multiply the difference in switches by 200 ms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ABABABAB has 7 switches and AAAABBBB has 1; the extra 6 switches cost 6 × 200 = 1,200 ms.

questions.onCorrect: Both have eight trials, so only the switches differ: six more switches, each at the same cost.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the cost of one switch. How many more switches does the alternating order have?
That is the whole switch cost of the alternating order. The blocked order has a switch too.

questions.prompt: In the study, 5 of 200 drivers showed no cost from doing a demanding task while driving. What percentage is that?
hints: Divide the supertaskers by the total tested.
The total is 200.
Convert 5/200 to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Five in two hundred is a very small share: nearly everyone paid a cost for doing two things.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count of drivers. Turn it into a percentage of all those tested.
That is the share who showed a cost. The question asks about those who showed none.

questions.prompt: Each trial takes 500 ms and each change of task adds 150 ms. How long does AABBAABB take, in milliseconds?
hints: Look for each place where A is followed by B or B by A.
There are eight trials at 500 ms each.
Add the switch costs to 4,000 ms.
questions.onCorrect: Trial time plus switch time, with only the changes of task counted as switches.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the trials. Add the cost of each change of task.
Read the sequence again. It changes task fewer times than that.

questions.prompt: An observer concentrating on a task fails to see a clearly visible but unexpected object. What is this failure called?
hints: It is a kind of blindness caused by where attention was directed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inattentional blindness: the object was visible but not attended.

questions.onCorrect: The object was visible but not attended, so it went unseen. That is inattentional blindness.

misconceptions.feedback: Change blindness is missing a change between two views. Here the object was never attended.

questions.prompt: What is the combined estimate, in millimetres?
hints: Reliability is one over the variance, 1/SD².
Vision's share is its reliability divided by the sum of both.
Multiply each reading by its share and add.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Weights 1/4 and 1/16 give vision 0.25/0.3125 = 0.8; estimate = 0.8 × 50 + 0.2 × 56 = 51.2 mm.

questions.onCorrect: Weights follow 1 ÷ SD², so the steadier cue counts for more than the midpoint would give it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain midpoint. The steadier cue should count for more.
That gives the larger weight to touch, but touch is the less reliable cue here.

questions.prompt: What is the combined estimate, in millimetres?
hints: The more reliable cue now is touch.
Combine 0.2 of the vision reading with the rest from touch.
questions.onCorrect: Touch is now the steadier cue, so it carries most of the weight and pulls the estimate towards its reading.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain midpoint. The steadier cue should count for more.
That uses the earlier weights. The steadier cue has changed.

questions.prompt: What is the standard deviation of the combined estimate, in millimetres?
hints: Add the two reliabilities 1/9 and 1/16.
Use the common denominator 144.
Take one over the square root of the sum.
questions.onCorrect: Add the reliabilities, then invert: the combined SD sits below both cues.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain average of the two SDs. Combining cues does better than averaging.
That adds the squares of the SDs and takes the root, which makes a wider spread. The formula adds reliabilities, 1 ÷ SD².

questions.prompt: You expect a line to be upright at 0° (SD 1°). You glimpse it at 10° (SD 3°). Combining expectation and glimpse by reliability, what tilt do you perceive, in degrees?
hints: Treat the expectation as a cue with its own SD.
The expectation's weight is 1/(1 + 1/9).
Only the glimpse's share multiplies a non-zero reading.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Reliabilities 1 and 1/9 give the expectation weight 0.9; perceived tilt = 0.9 × 0 + 0.1 × 10 = 1°.

questions.onCorrect: The steadier expectation carries most of the weight, so what you see is pulled almost to upright.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the midpoint of expectation and glimpse. The steadier one should count for more.
That gives the larger weight to the glimpse, but the expectation is the steadier cue.

questions.prompt: Hearing places a voice 10° to the right (SD 8°); vision places the moving lips at 0° (SD 4°). Where is the voice heard, in degrees to the right?
hints: Compute 1/SD² for each sense.
Hearing's weight is its reliability over the total.
Multiply that weight by 10°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Reliabilities 1/64 and 1/16 give hearing weight (1/64)/(5/64) = 0.2; location = 0.2 × 10 = 2°. Vision captures the sound, as in ventriloquism.

questions.onCorrect: Hearing is the less reliable sense, so vision pulls the heard location towards the lips. This is the ventriloquist effect.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the midpoint. Vision is steadier, so it should count for more.
That gives most of the weight to hearing, the less reliable sense.

questions.prompt: Perception guided by knowledge and expectation, rather than built only from incoming sensory features, is called what kind of processing?
hints: It runs in the opposite direction to bottom-up processing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Top-down processing: knowledge and expectation shape what is perceived.

questions.onCorrect: Knowledge and expectation shape what is perceived. That is top-down, the reverse of building from features.

misconceptions.feedback: Bottom-up builds perception from the incoming features alone. This asks for the opposite direction.

questions.prompt: How many digits exceed the limit?
hints: Each separate digit counts as one chunk.
Compare the number of chunks with the capacity.
Subtract the capacity from the number of digits.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nine chunks against a capacity of four leaves 9 − 4 = 5 beyond the limit.

questions.onCorrect: Nine chunks against a capacity of four leaves the difference beyond the limit.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every digit. Only those beyond what the store can hold exceed the limit.
That is the capacity. The question asks how many are over it.

questions.prompt: How many more letters can they hold by chunking than by storing one letter per chunk?
hints: Find how many letters fit when each chunk is an acronym.
Find how many fit when each chunk is one letter.
Subtract the second from the first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four acronym chunks hold 12 letters; four single-letter chunks hold 4; the gain is 8.

questions.onCorrect: Each chunk holds a whole acronym, so the same four chunks carry far more letters.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number held by chunking. The question asks for the extra over one letter per chunk.
That is how many letters fit without chunking. Find the gain over that.

questions.prompt: A chess master recalls a 20-piece position as 4 chunks. On average, how many pieces are in each chunk?
hints: Average means total pieces shared equally across chunks.
There are 20 pieces in the position.
Divide by the number of chunks.
questions.onCorrect: The master's chunks are rich, with several pieces in each. Capacity stays ordinary.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of chunks. The question asks how many pieces each one holds.
That subtracts instead of sharing the pieces out equally.

questions.prompt: Lists of similar-sounding words are harder to recall in order. Which part of Baddeley and Hitch's working-memory model does this point to?
hints: The interference comes from sound.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The phonological loop stores speech-based codes, so similar sounds interfere with one another.

choices.label: Phonological loop
Visuospatial sketchpad
Central executive
Episodic buffer

questions.onCorrect: Similar sounds interfere in the speech-based store, so similar-sounding words are recalled worse.

misconceptions.feedback: The sketchpad holds images and positions, not sound.
The central executive directs attention. It does not store sound.
The episodic buffer links the other parts. The interference here comes from sound.

questions.prompt: A 16-digit card number is printed in groups of four. If each group becomes one chunk, how many chunks must be held?
hints: Each printed group becomes a single chunk.
Find how many groups of four make 16.
Divide 16 by the group size.
questions.onCorrect: Each printed group becomes one chunk, so sixteen digits become only a few chunks.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the digits. Each group of four is one chunk.
That is the number of digits left after one group. Divide the digits by the size of a group.

questions.prompt: What is the strategy of organising items into meaningful groups so more fits in short-term memory called?
hints: The groups are called chunks.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chunking: grouping items into units already known from long-term memory.

questions.onCorrect: Chunking groups items into units already known, so more fits within the same limit.

misconceptions.feedback: Rehearsal repeats items. The strategy asked about groups them into units.

questions.prompt: What percentage recall does the curve predict 90 days after learning?
hints: Compute 9S first.
Divide t by 9S.
Substitute into 1/(1 + t/9S) and convert to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Divide the days by 9S and put it in the curve: here the ratio reaches one and recall has halved.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of days. Put t ÷ 9S into the curve to get a percentage.
That divides t by S. The curve divides by nine times S.

questions.prompt: What percentage recall is predicted 13.5 days after that review?
hints: Multiply the stability by 9.
Divide 13.5 by that product.
Take one over one plus your answer.
questions.onCorrect: The review raised stability, so 9S is bigger and t ÷ 9S is smaller: recall stays high.

misconceptions.feedback: That stops after t ÷ 9S. Put it in the curve to get recall.
That is the share forgotten. The question asks for the share recalled.

questions.prompt: A card has stability 12 days. If reviews are scheduled for when predicted recall falls to 90%, how many days after its last review is it due?
hints: Recall the definition of stability.
The 90% target matches that definition exactly.
The interval equals the stability.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Stability is defined as the interval at which predicted recall reaches 90%, so the card is due in 12 days.

questions.onCorrect: Stability is the days to reach the 90% target, so the card is due after that many days.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the target recall, not a number of days.
That multiplies by nine. The definition of S already includes the 90% target.

questions.prompt: A week after studying, students who practised recall remembered 56% of idea units and students who reread remembered 42%. How many percentage points higher was recall practice?
hints: Compare the two one-week scores.
Percentage points are a plain difference of percentages.
Subtract the rereading score from the recall-practice score.
questions.onCorrect: Recall practice looked worse early but lasted longer. The gap is a plain difference of the two scores.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one of the two scores. The question asks how far apart they are.
Percentage points are a difference, not a sum.

questions.prompt: A memory has stability S = 4 days. Using R = 1/(1 + t/9S), what percentage recall is predicted 108 days after learning?
hints: Multiply S by 9.
Divide 108 by that result.
Take one over one plus the quotient.
questions.onCorrect: Divide the days by 9S, then put the ratio in the curve. A longer wait with smaller stability leaves less recall.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share forgotten. The question asks for the share still recalled.
That is t ÷ 9S, not recall. Put it into the curve.

questions.prompt: Studying in short sessions spread over days, rather than one long session, is called what kind of practice?
hints: It is the opposite of massed practice, or cramming.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Distributed, or spaced, practice.

questions.onCorrect: Spreading study over days is distributed, or spaced, practice, the opposite of cramming.

misconceptions.feedback: Massed practice is one long session. The question asks about study spread across days.

questions.prompt: What is V after two pairings?
hints: Work one trial at a time.
The first trial adds 0.3 × (1 − 0).
On trial two the remaining gap is 1 − 0.3.
questions.onCorrect: The second step closes the same share of a smaller gap, so V grows more slowly the more it has.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the first step twice. The second step is smaller because less gap is left.
That is the value after only the first pairing.

questions.prompt: Starting from V = 0, what is the final V?
hints: Compute the two pairings first.
On the bell-alone trial the target is 0.
Move V halfway towards 0 from its value after two pairings.
questions.onCorrect: On the bell-alone trial V moves a share of the way towards 0: unlearning that is partial, not total.

misconceptions.feedback: That is V before the bell-alone trial. The final trial changes it.
That wipes out all learning. The rule moves V only part of the way to the target.

questions.prompt: A pigeon on a fixed-ratio 5 schedule makes 30 pecks. How many rewards does it earn?
hints: Fixed ratio 5 means a fixed number of responses per reward.
Count how many complete sets of five fit in 30.
Divide 30 by 5.
questions.onCorrect: Every fifth response pays, so divide the responses by the ratio.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies. Each reward needs five responses, so divide instead.
That subtracts the ratio once. Count how many sets of five fit in the total.

questions.prompt: On a fixed-interval 10-second schedule, a rat presses every 3 seconds for 60 seconds. The first press at least 10 s after the previous reward is rewarded. How many rewards does it earn?
hints: The first press at or after 10 s is at 12 s.
The next must come at least 10 s after 12 s.
Keep stepping until 60 s and count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Rewarded presses fall at 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 s: five rewards.

questions.onCorrect: Only presses can be rewarded, and presses fall every 3 seconds, so each reward lands a little after the interval.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the time by the interval. A reward needs a press, and presses come every 3 seconds.
That is the number of presses, not the number of rewards.

questions.prompt: A slot machine pays out after an unpredictable number of plays, averaging one win in twenty. Which reinforcement schedule is this?
hints: Decide whether rewards depend on time or on the number of responses, and whether that number is predictable.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Variable ratio: rewards follow an unpredictable number of responses.

questions.onCorrect: Rewards after an unpredictable number of responses form a variable-ratio schedule, the hardest to extinguish.

misconceptions.feedback: Fixed means the same number every time. This payout is unpredictable.
An interval depends on time. This payout depends on the number of plays.

questions.prompt: A child's screen time is taken away after they hit a sibling, and the hitting becomes less frequent. Which consequence is this?
hints: Ask whether something was added or removed, and whether the behaviour rose or fell.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Something pleasant is removed (negative) and the behaviour decreases (punishment).

choices.label: Negative punishment
Positive punishment
Negative reinforcement
Positive reinforcement

questions.onCorrect: Something pleasant was removed and the behaviour fell: that is negative punishment.

misconceptions.feedback: Positive punishment adds something unpleasant. Here something pleasant was taken away.
Negative reinforcement makes the behaviour more likely. Here it became less frequent.
Positive reinforcement adds something pleasant and the behaviour rises. Here it fell.

questions.prompt: How many false positives are there?
hints: First find how many people do not have the disease.
Subtract the 1% who have it from 1,000.
Take 10% of that number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1,000 − 10 = 990 people do not have the disease; 10% of 990 = 99 false positives.

questions.onCorrect: False positives come only from people without the disease, a much bigger group than those who have it.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes the error rate of the wrong group. False positives come from people who do not have the disease.
That takes the error rate of everyone. False positives come only from those who do not have the disease.

questions.prompt: What is the probability, as a percentage, that a person who tests positive has the disease? Give one decimal place.
hints: Restrict attention to people who tested positive.
The true positives are the people in that group who have the disease.
Divide 9 by the total number of positives and round.
questions.onCorrect: True positives over all positives, not the test's hit rate: most positives here are false alarms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the test's hit rate. The question asks how many positives are right.
That is the number of true positives. Turn it into a share of all positives.
That divides by the false positives alone. Divide by everyone flagged.

questions.prompt: What percentage of positive results are true positives?
hints: Count the people with and without the disease first.
Apply 90% to the first group and 10% to the second.
Divide true positives by all positives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 have it and 90 test positive; 900 do not and 90 test positive; 90/180 = 50%.

questions.onCorrect: The same test, a different base rate: true positives now equal false positives, so a positive is a coin toss.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the hit rate. The question asks what share of positives are true.
That is the share who have the disease. Ask how many positives are true.

questions.prompt: 20% of a city's cabs are blue. A witness who names colours correctly 75% of the time says the cab was blue. What is the probability, as a percentage, that it was blue? Give one decimal place.
hints: Imagine 1,000 cabs: 200 blue and 800 green.
The witness calls 75% of blue cabs blue and 25% of green cabs blue.
Divide correct 'blue' calls by all 'blue' calls.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Per 1,000 cabs: 150 blue cabs called blue and 200 green cabs called blue; 150/350 = 42.9%.

questions.onCorrect: Count the cabs the witness calls blue: true calls over all calls. The many green cabs produce many wrong calls.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the witness's accuracy, not the chance that this cab was blue.
That is the base rate alone. The witness's report adds evidence.
That is the share of 'blue' calls that were wrong.

questions.prompt: 2,000 people are tested for a condition that 5% have. The test detects 80% of cases and gives false positives for 10% of people without it. How many people test positive in total?
hints: 5% of 2,000 have the condition.
Find the true positives and the false positives separately.
Add the two groups of positives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 have it, 80 test positive; 1,900 do not, 190 test positive; 80 + 190 = 270.

questions.onCorrect: Add the true positives and the false positives: the flagged group is everyone with a positive result.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the true positives. Add the false positives too.
That counts only the false positives. Add the true positives too.

questions.prompt: A doctor judges a positive result from a 90%-accurate test as 90% likely to be right, ignoring that the disease is rare. What is this error called?
hints: The neglected number is how common the condition is to begin with.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Base-rate neglect: the prior frequency of the condition is ignored.

questions.onCorrect: Ignoring how rare a condition is when judging a result is base-rate neglect.

misconceptions.feedback: Confirmation bias favours evidence that fits what you believe. This error ignores how common the condition is.

questions.prompt: By how many percentage points did the two median guesses differ?
hints: Compare the two median estimates, not the anchors.
The higher anchor produced the higher median.
Subtract the low-anchor median from the high-anchor median.
questions.onCorrect: A wheel everyone knew was random still moved the typical guess by 20 points.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one of the medians. The question asks how far apart the two medians are.
That is the gap between the anchors. Compare the medians.

questions.prompt: What is the anchoring index, (difference in medians) ÷ (difference in anchors)?
hints: Find the gap between the median estimates.
Find the gap between the anchors.
Divide the first gap by the second.
questions.onCorrect: The estimates moved a share of the way the anchors did: a clear pull, but not a full one.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap in medians alone. Divide it by the gap between the anchors.
That divides the gap between anchors by the gap in medians. Invert it.

questions.prompt: In a sample of 600 English words containing k, 200 start with k and 400 have k as the third letter. What percentage start with k? Give one decimal place.
hints: Divide words starting with k by all the k-words.
The denominator is 600.
Convert to a percentage and round to one decimal place.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 200/600 = 0.333, or 33.3%: words with k third are twice as common, though harder to recall.

questions.onCorrect: A third start with k. The other two thirds are harder to recall, so they feel rarer.

misconceptions.feedback: That compares the 200 with the 400 alone. Compare it with all 600.
That is the share with k as the third letter. The question asks about words that start with k.

questions.prompt: How much does the ball cost, in pence?
hints: Write the bat's price in terms of the ball's.
The two prices add to 110p.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ball x, bat x + 100p: 2x + 100 = 110, so x = 5p. The intuitive 10p would make the total £1.20.

questions.onCorrect: Write the bat's price in terms of the ball's, then solve: the quick answer fails the check.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the answer that springs to mind. Check it: the bat must cost £1.00 more, so the total would be too high.
That is the total of both. The ball is only part of it.

questions.prompt: Anchors of 100 and 500 produce median estimates of 220 and 340. What is the anchoring index?
hints: The index compares how far estimates moved with how far anchors moved.
Estimates moved 120.
Divide by the difference between the anchors.
questions.onCorrect: Estimates moved a share of the anchors' gap: divide the first difference by the second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap in medians alone. Divide it by the gap between anchors.
That divides the gap between anchors by the gap in medians. Invert it.

questions.prompt: After several news reports of shark attacks, a swimmer judges sharks a bigger risk than drowning. Judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind is which heuristic?
hints: The examples are readily available in memory.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The availability heuristic: vivid, easily recalled cases feel common.

questions.onCorrect: Vivid, easily recalled cases feel common. That is the availability heuristic.

misconceptions.feedback: Anchoring is the pull of a starting number. This is about how easily examples come to mind.

questions.prompt: What percentage of all the critical answers conformed? Give one decimal place.
hints: First find the total number of critical answers.
Multiply people by critical answers each.
Divide 72 by that total and convert to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Divide the conforming answers by all critical answers: people times answers each.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count of conforming answers. Turn it into a percentage of all critical answers.
That is the total number of critical answers. The percentage is the conforming share of it.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the 40 volunteers obeyed to the end?
hints: Divide the number who continued by the number tested.
The denominator is 40.
Convert 26/40 to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Divide the number who continued by the number tested to get the obedience rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count. Turn it into a percentage of the 40 participants.
That is the share who stopped earlier. The question asks about those who continued.

questions.prompt: In the first version 26 of 40 volunteers obeyed to the end, and with the volunteer's hand pressing the learner's onto the plate 12 of 40 did. By how many percentage points did obedience fall?
hints: Turn each count into a percentage.
Both conditions had 40 participants.
Subtract the touch-proximity percentage from the baseline percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Turn each count into a percentage, then subtract: closeness to the victim cut obedience sharply.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the baseline rate alone. Subtract the touch-proximity rate from it.
That is the touch-proximity rate alone. Find the gap between the two rates.
That is a difference in people. The question asks for percentage points.

questions.prompt: What is the probability, as a percentage, that at least one of the five acts? Give one decimal place.
hints: Find the chance that one person does not act.
Multiply that chance by itself once per bystander.
Subtract the result from 1 and convert to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Find the chance that nobody acts, then subtract it from 1: independent chances do not add.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance that nobody acts. The question asks about at least one.
That adds the five probabilities. Chances of independent events do not add.

questions.prompt: Three bystanders each independently help with probability 0.5. What is the probability, as a percentage, that at least one helps?
hints: Work out the chance that nobody helps.
Each bystander fails to help with probability 0.5.
Subtract 0.5³ from 1 and convert to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Find the chance that nobody helps, then subtract it from 1 to get the chance that at least one does.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance that nobody helps. The question asks about at least one.
That adds the probabilities. Chances of independent events do not add.

questions.prompt: Which statement fits the evidence from CCTV recordings of real public conflicts?
hints: The recordings counted whether anyone at all stepped in.

acceptedIdeas: Someone usually intervenes, and more bystanders make intervention more likely
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Philpot and colleagues (2020) found intervention in 91% of 219 conflicts, rising with the number of bystanders.

choices.label: Someone usually intervenes, and more bystanders make intervention more likely
Bystanders almost never intervene in public conflicts
Each extra bystander halves the chance that anyone helps

questions.onCorrect: Footage of real conflicts shows that someone usually steps in, and more onlookers make it more likely.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the myth the footage challenges. Look at how often someone stepped in.
No such halving was found. Look at how intervention changed as the crowd grew.

questions.prompt: A pen and a notebook cost £2.20 together. The notebook costs £2.00 more than the pen. How much does the pen cost, in pence?
hints: Write the notebook's price in terms of the pen's.
The two prices add to 220p.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Pen x, notebook x + 200: 2x + 200 = 220, so x = 10p.

questions.onCorrect: Check the quick answer against the total: the pen is 10p and the notebook £2.10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the answer that springs to mind. Check it: the notebook would then cost £2.20 alone.
That is the total of both. The pen is only part of it.

questions.prompt: Which jacket is more likely to feel like a bargain?
hints: Which price tag gives you another number to compare with?
Does the £200 change how £120 looks?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The one with the “was £200” tag: the higher number makes £120 feel low.

choices.label: The one shown at £120 alone
They feel the same.
The one marked “was £200, now £120”

questions.onCorrect: A number you meet first colours the next. You spotted the effect of a starting number before it had a name.

misconceptions.feedback: Check which price tag gives you a number to compare against.
The two tags give you different numbers to compare, so they need not feel the same.

questions.prompt: What made the wheel experiment striking?
hints: Would you expect a spinning wheel to tell you anything about the United Nations?

acceptedIdeas: The number was plainly random, yet it still moved estimates.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The wheel was plainly random, yet it still pulled the estimates.

choices.label: The number was plainly random, yet it still moved estimates.
People knew the true answer and ignored the wheel.
The wheel gave people useful information.

questions.onCorrect: A number that everyone knew to be random still pulled the estimates towards it.

misconceptions.feedback: If they had ignored it, the estimates would not have differed by anchor.
The wheel was rigged and plainly meaningless.

questions.prompt: Anchors of 0 and 40 produce median estimates of 10 and 30. What is the anchoring index?
hints: Find the gap between the medians.
Find the gap between the anchors.
Divide the first gap by the second.
questions.onCorrect: The estimates moved half as far as the anchors did.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap in medians alone. Divide it by the gap between anchors.
That divides the gap between anchors by the gap in medians. Invert it.

questions.prompt: What does an index of 0.35 say about the anchors?
hints: Think about what an index of 0 means, and what an index of 1 means.

acceptedIdeas: The medians moved about a third as far as the anchors did.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An index between 0 and 1 shows how far the estimates moved, as a share of the anchors' gap.

choices.label: The anchors were ignored completely.
The medians moved about a third as far as the anchors did.
The medians moved exactly as far as the anchors.

questions.onCorrect: An index of 0.35 means about a third of the anchors' gap showed up in the estimates.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be an index of 0.
That would be an index of 1.

questions.prompt: Each trial takes 500 ms and each change of task adds 150 ms. How many milliseconds faster is AAAABBBB than AABBAABB?
hints: Both have eight trials, so only the switches differ.
Count the switches in each sequence.
Multiply the difference in switches by the cost of one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: AABBAABB has 3 switches and AAAABBBB has 1. The 2 extra switches cost 2 × 150 = 300 ms.

questions.onCorrect: Equal trials mean only switches differ: two extra switches at the same cost each.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole switch cost of the mixed order. The blocked order has a switch too.
That is the cost of one switch. How many extra switches are there?

questions.prompt: Which order will take less time?
hints: Each card takes the same time. What else is going on between cards?
Think about what happens in your head each time the kind of job changes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sums first, then words: the job changes only once, so the mind reconfigures only once.

choices.label: Swapping between a sum and a word each time
Sums first, then words
They will take the same time.

questions.onCorrect: Changing job costs time on top of the work itself. You reasoned out a switch cost before it had a name.

misconceptions.feedback: Every swap makes you change the kind of job. That is extra work beyond the cards themselves.
The cards take equal time, but the changes between jobs do not come free.

questions.prompt: Which statement does inattentional blindness support?
hints: The object in the study was in plain view.

acceptedIdeas: Looking at something does not guarantee that you see it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Looking is not seeing: an object in plain view can be missed if attention is elsewhere.

choices.label: People with poor eyesight cannot see unexpected things.
Looking at something does not guarantee that you see it.
Unexpected objects are always invisible.

questions.onCorrect: Attention decides what you notice, so something in plain view can still be missed.

misconceptions.feedback: The viewers had ordinary eyesight. The cause was where their attention was.
Many did see it. It was missed only by those attending elsewhere.

questions.prompt: How many switches are in the sequence ABBA?
hints: A switch is a change from one task to the other.
Read the sequence from left to right.
Count the places where the letter changes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A to B, then B to A: two switches. B to B is not a switch.

questions.onCorrect: A switch is a change of task: A to B and B to A. Repeating B costs nothing extra.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only one of the two changes. Read the sequence left to right.
That counts the gap between every pair of trials. Repeats are not switches.

questions.prompt: In the sequence AABAB, why are there 3 switches in 5 trials?
hints: Look at each pair of neighbouring trials. Is the task different?

acceptedIdeas: Only a change from one task to the other counts, and the first two trials are the same task.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only a change of task is a switch. Two As in a row are not.

choices.label: Every trial after the first counts as a switch.
Every second trial is a switch.
Only a change from one task to the other counts, and the first two trials are the same task.

questions.onCorrect: Only changes of task count. A repeated task adds no switch cost.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be four, and it ignores that the first two trials match.
Switches depend on the sequence, not on every other trial.

questions.prompt: Of 1,000 people, 5% have a condition. The test flags 80% of cases and 10% of people without it. What percentage of positive results are correct? Give one decimal place.
hints: Count the people with and without the condition.
Find the true positives and the false positives separately.
Divide the true positives by all positives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 50 have it and 40 test positive; 950 do not and 95 test positive. 40 ÷ 135 = 0.296, or 29.6%.

questions.onCorrect: True positives over all positives: even a good test is wrong most of the time when the condition is rare.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the hit rate. The question asks what share of positives are right.
That is the number of true positives. Turn it into a share of all positives.

questions.prompt: A bag beeps. Roughly how likely is it that it holds the banned item?
hints: Count how many bags beep in total.
Of all the bags that beep, how many hold the banned item?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 2 in 100: 2 true beeps among 100 bags that beep.

choices.label: About 2 in 100
About 50-50
About 98 in 100

questions.onCorrect: Counting the beeps shows that most are false alarms. You used natural frequencies without being told.

misconceptions.feedback: Count how many bags beep and how many of those are real.
That is the scanner's success rate on bags that hold the item, not the chance that a beeping bag does.

questions.prompt: Of 500 people, 4% have a condition. How many people is that?
hints: A percentage of a group is a number of people.
Find 1% of 500 first.
Multiply that by 4.
questions.onCorrect: Work with people, not percentages: 4% of 500 is 20.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the percentage. Apply it to the 500 people.
That takes 20% of the group. Use the percentage given.

questions.prompt: A screening finds 4 true positives and 16 false positives. What percentage of the positive results are correct?
hints: The flagged group is the true positives plus the false positives.
Add 4 and 16.
Divide the true positives by that total.
questions.onCorrect: Divide true positives by all positives: here one in five positives is right.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the false positives alone. Divide by everyone flagged.
That is the share of positives that are wrong.

questions.prompt: Why divide by all 120 positives, not by the 50 people who have the disease?
hints: Who is the question about: everyone, or someone who tested positive?

acceptedIdeas: The person tested positive, so they are one of the 120 people flagged.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The question is about someone who tested positive, so the flagged group is the whole of the comparison.

choices.label: Because 120 is the bigger number.
Because the 50 people do not count.
The person tested positive, so they are one of the 120 people flagged.

questions.onCorrect: The person has tested positive, so they are one of the flagged. That group is the denominator.

misconceptions.feedback: Size does not decide the denominator. The question does.
The 50 are counted, as the true positives among the flagged.

questions.prompt: The rate is 0.6, the maximum is 1 and V starts at 0. What is V after two pairings?
hints: Work one trial at a time.
The first trial adds 0.6 × (1 − 0).
On trial two the remaining gap is 1 − 0.6.
questions.onCorrect: Each step closes the same share of what is left: 0.6, then 0.24 more.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the first step twice. The second step is smaller because less gap is left.
That multiplies by V, not by the gap. The gap is the maximum minus V.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of bell and food teaches the dog the most?
hints: Think about how much is left to learn by each pairing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first: it starts from nothing, so there is the most left to learn.

choices.label: The fifth
The first
The tenth

questions.onCorrect: Learning is fastest at the start, when the most is left to learn. You reasoned out the shape of the learning curve.

misconceptions.feedback: Think about how much is left to learn by the fifth pairing.
Think about how much is left to learn by the tenth pairing.

questions.prompt: The rate is 0.5, the maximum is 1 and V starts at 0. What is V after one pairing?
hints: ΔV = rate × (λ − V).
Here λ − V is 1 − 0.
Multiply the rate by the gap.
questions.onCorrect: One pairing adds the rate times the whole gap, since V starts at zero.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats one pairing as learning everything. Each pairing closes only a share of the gap.
That multiplies the rate by itself. Multiply it by the gap instead.

questions.prompt: Why does V fall on a bell-alone trial?
hints: What does the bell now predict?

acceptedIdeas: With no food, the maximum is 0, so the gap is negative.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Without food the bell predicts nothing, so the maximum is 0 and the change is negative.

choices.label: The bell wears out with use.
With no food, the maximum is 0, so the gap is negative.
The dog forgets as time passes.

questions.onCorrect: No food means λ is 0. The gap is then negative, so V moves down.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule has no wear-out term. The change comes from the gap.
Time does not appear in the rule. The change comes from the gap.

questions.prompt: Praise follows a pupil raising a hand, and hand-raising becomes more frequent. Is this positive or negative reinforcement?
hints: Was something added or removed, and did the behaviour rise or fall?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Positive reinforcement: praise is added and the behaviour rises.

questions.onCorrect: Something was added and the behaviour rose, so it is positive reinforcement.

misconceptions.feedback: Negative means something is removed. Was anything removed here?
Punishment makes the behaviour less likely. Here it became more frequent.

questions.prompt: A teacher recalls that rainy days bring rowdy classes. Counted properly, 9 of 30 rainy days were rowdy and 40 of 100 dry days were. By how many percentage points is the rowdy rate higher on dry days?
hints: Turn each count into a rate.
Divide the rowdy days by all days in each group.
Subtract the smaller rate from the larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 9/30 = 30% and 40/100 = 40%, so the gap is 40 − 30 = 10 percentage points.

questions.onCorrect: Compare rates in every group. The rainy days only felt more rowdy.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the raw counts, but the groups differ in size. Turn each count into a rate first.
That is one of the rates, not the gap between them.

questions.prompt: Ice-cream takings and pool rescues in a seaside town rise and fall together through the summer. What best explains why?
hints: Ask what else changes across the year.
Sales and rescues are both highest in the same weeks. What do those weeks have in common?

acceptedIdeas: Hot weather brings more people to both the ice-cream van and the pool.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Hot weather: it brings more people to the ice-cream van and to the pool.

choices.label: Eating ice cream makes swimmers more likely to need rescuing.
Hot weather brings more people to both the ice-cream van and the pool.
Rescues make onlookers want ice cream.

questions.onCorrect: Something outside both lists moves them together. The next screen gives that hidden driver a name.

misconceptions.feedback: Possible, but the pattern alone does not show it. Ask what else changes through the year.
That reverses the arrow, and nothing in the pattern points that way. Look for something that changes both.

questions.prompt: Is a correlation of r = −0.6 stronger or weaker than one of r = +0.4?
hints: Strength is the distance from zero. Ignore the sign when you compare.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stronger: r = −0.6 is further from zero. The minus sign only gives direction.

questions.onCorrect: Strength is distance from zero, so −0.6 is stronger than +0.4. The sign only gives the direction.

misconceptions.feedback: A plus sign shows direction, not strength. Compare the sizes with the signs set aside.

questions.prompt: Two measures correlate at r = 0.5. What percentage of their variation do they have in common?
hints: Squaring r gives the shared share.
Multiply 0.5 by itself.
Convert the decimal to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: r² = 0.5² = 0.25, so 25% of the variation is shared.

questions.onCorrect: Square r, then read it as a percentage: 0.5 × 0.5 is a quarter, or 25%.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads r as a percentage. The share comes from squaring it first.
That divides r by ten rather than squaring it.

questions.prompt: Children with bigger shoe sizes read better. Name the most likely confound.
hints: A confound is a third variable that drives both measures. What changes both shoe size and reading skill?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Age drives both measures: older children have bigger feet and better reading.

questions.onCorrect: Age moves both measures together. A confound sits behind the pattern, not between the two measures.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one of the two measures. The question asks for a third variable behind both.

questions.prompt: Why does holding temperature roughly fixed make the link disappear?
hints: What changed from day to day in the first picture? What changes in the second?

acceptedIdeas: Temperature was what moved sales and rescues together, so once it is fixed nothing is left to move them together.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Temperature moved both measures; fixed, it cannot.

choices.label: Ice-cream sales stop mattering once the days are warm.
A smaller set of days always shows a weaker correlation.
Temperature was what moved sales and rescues together, so once it is fixed nothing is left to move them together.

questions.onCorrect: Fixing the confound removes what linked the two measures. That is what a confound does.

misconceptions.feedback: Sales never mattered to rescues in the first place. The question is what linked them.
Fewer days alone do not weaken a real link. Something specific stopped the pattern.

questions.prompt: A course lifts scores by 6 points in two classes. Scores in class A usually differ from the class average by about 3 points, and in class B by about 30. In which class is the 6-point gain more impressive?
hints: Think about how easily a 6-point gain could be noise.
In which class would a 6-point change stand out from the usual variation?

acceptedIdeas: Class A, where scores vary little
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Class A: against a spread of about 3 points, a 6-point gain is large.

choices.label: Class B, where scores vary a lot
Class A, where scores vary little
Both are equally impressive, because the gain is the same size.

questions.onCorrect: A gain is measured against the scatter of scores. Beside a spread of 3, a gain of 6 stands out.

misconceptions.feedback: With a spread of about 30, a 6-point gain is lost in the ordinary variation.
The same raw gain means different things beside different spreads.

questions.prompt: A training course raises scores by 8 points, and scores spread with a standard deviation of 20. What is Cohen's d?
hints: d measures a difference in units of standard deviation.
Divide the difference between the means by the spread.
Divide 8 by 20.
questions.onCorrect: d is a gap between means counted in standard deviations: eight points against a spread of twenty.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the raw difference. d measures it against the spread.
That divides the spread by the difference. d divides the difference by the spread.

questions.prompt: Why not simply average the two standard deviations?
hints: Which of the two groups has more spread, and which number should count for more?

acceptedIdeas: The pooled SD is built from the variances, so the group with more spread counts for more.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The pooled SD is built from variances, so the more spread-out group counts for more.

choices.label: Standard deviations can never be averaged.
Squaring is needed only to make the numbers positive.
The pooled SD is built from the variances, so the group with more spread counts for more.

questions.onCorrect: Working from the squares lets the more spread-out group count for more, as it does in the data.

misconceptions.feedback: Averaging is allowed. The pooled value is simply a better combination here.
Standard deviations are already positive. Squaring serves another purpose.

questions.prompt: A small study chases a small effect. What is most likely?
hints: Think about how much noise a few people add.

acceptedIdeas: It will often miss the effect, and a lucky find will overstate it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With little power, a real small effect is often missed. Those found are usually overestimates.

choices.label: It will often miss the effect, and a lucky find will overstate it.
It will find the effect as often as a large study would.
It will always miss the effect.

questions.onCorrect: Low power means real effects are often missed, and the hits tend to be lucky overestimates.

misconceptions.feedback: Sample size drives power. A small study has much less of it.
A small study sometimes finds it. When it does, the estimate is usually too big.

questions.prompt: What is it called when a study is repeated with fresh participants to see whether its result holds?
hints: The word is in the headline of this screen.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Replication: repeating a study with new participants.

questions.onCorrect: A replication repeats a study with fresh participants. One result is weak evidence until it has been repeated.

misconceptions.feedback: Reanalysis reuses the same data. This asks for repeating the study with new participants.

questions.prompt: What is the best reply to the friend?
hints: Think about who is likely to sign up for a fitness programme.
Were the two groups equally fit before the programme began?

acceptedIdeas: Not necessarily: fitter members may have been the ones who chose to join.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Not necessarily: fitter members may have been the ones who chose to join.

choices.label: Yes: if joiners are fitter, the programme has worked.
Only if the joiners lost weight.
Not necessarily: fitter members may have been the ones who chose to join.

questions.onCorrect: People who choose a programme differ from those who do not. You spotted that before anyone gave it a name.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the final gap as the programme's work. Ask who chose to join in the first place.
Weight is one possible outcome, but it does not fix who chose to join.

questions.prompt: Why is a one-point gap before the study no problem for random assignment?
hints: Does one draw guarantee equal groups, or only fairness?

acceptedIdeas: It promises no trait systematically favours one group, not that the groups are identical.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Random assignment promises fairness, not equality in one small study.

choices.label: Because random assignment makes the groups exactly identical.
It promises no trait systematically favours one group, not that the groups are identical.
Because the treatment will cancel the gap.

questions.onCorrect: Chance gaps are expected in a small study. Random assignment only ensures no trait leans one way.

misconceptions.feedback: One draw of eight people cannot make groups identical. The gap just seen proves that.
The treatment has not been given yet. The gap exists before it.

questions.prompt: Which is the best operational definition of “fitness”?
hints: An operational definition states exactly what will be measured.

acceptedIdeas: The distance a person covers in a 12-minute run
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The distance covered in a 12-minute run is a precise measurement anyone could repeat.

choices.label: How athletic a person looks to the researcher
How fit a person says they feel
The distance a person covers in a 12-minute run

questions.onCorrect: A good operational definition is a measurement someone else could repeat exactly.

misconceptions.feedback: That depends on opinion, so two researchers could disagree. Choose a measurement.
That relies on a feeling, not a measurement anyone could repeat.

questions.prompt: Why give the control group an identical-looking pill with no active ingredient?
hints: What else, besides the drug, might make people improve?

acceptedIdeas: So that expectation is the same in both groups
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It keeps expectation equal, so only the active ingredient differs between the groups.

choices.label: So that expectation is the same in both groups
So that the control group cannot improve
So that the drug group takes longer to improve

questions.onCorrect: Equal pills mean equal expectation. Only the active ingredient then differs between groups.

misconceptions.feedback: The control group can still improve through expectation and time. That is the point of the pill.
The pill is about what people expect, not how long they take.

questions.prompt: A memory has stability 6 days. A successful review multiplies stability by 3. How many days after that review is the card next due, when recall falls to 90%?
hints: First find the new stability.
The interval equals the stability.
Multiply 6 by the growth factor.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The new stability is 6 × 3 = 18 days, and a card is due when recall falls to 90%, which is S days after the review.

questions.onCorrect: Success multiplies stability, and the card is due S days later, so the gap widens.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the old stability. A successful review has raised it.
That adds 3 instead of multiplying by it.

questions.prompt: Over the next day, what is most likely to happen?
hints: Is the loss steady, or does it slow down once the weakest memories are gone?
What has already been forgotten cannot be forgotten twice.

acceptedIdeas: You lose fewer than the 40 you lost on the first day.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: You lose fewer than 40: forgetting is fast at first and slows as time passes.

choices.label: You lose about another 40.
You lose most of the 60 that are left.
You lose fewer than the 40 you lost on the first day.

questions.onCorrect: Forgetting slows as the weakest memories go first. You predicted the shape of the curve.

misconceptions.feedback: That assumes a steady rate of loss. The loss is greatest at the start.
Losing most of the remainder would make the second day worse than the first. The loss tends to be gentler.

questions.prompt: A memory has stability 2 days. How many days until its predicted recall falls to 90%?
hints: Recall the definition of stability.
Stability is measured in days.
Stability is the number of days until recall falls to 90%.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Stability is the days until recall falls to 90%, so 2 days.

questions.onCorrect: Stability is, by definition, the days until predicted recall falls to 90%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is when this memory halves. The question asks about the 90% point.
That multiplies by nine. The definition of S already marks the 90% point.

questions.prompt: After a successful review, what happens to the next gap?
hints: Stability goes up after a success.

acceptedIdeas: The memory fades more slowly, so the next review can wait longer.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A success raises stability, so the curve flattens and the next gap grows.

choices.label: The memory fades faster, so reviews must be closer together.
Nothing changes, because every review is the same.
The memory fades more slowly, so the next review can wait longer.

questions.onCorrect: Success raises stability. A flatter curve means the next review can wait longer.

misconceptions.feedback: A success strengthens the memory. It does not make it more fragile.
Each success changes the stability, so the gaps can grow.

questions.prompt: Why does a larger stability slow forgetting?
hints: Look at which number sits under the fraction.

acceptedIdeas: It makes 9S bigger, so t ÷ 9S grows more slowly as days pass.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A larger S makes 9S bigger, so t ÷ 9S grows slowly and recall stays high longer.

choices.label: It makes 9S bigger, so t ÷ 9S grows more slowly as days pass.
It makes t smaller, so fewer days have passed.
It adds a fixed amount to recall.

questions.onCorrect: S sits under the fraction. A bigger S makes the ratio grow more slowly, so recall holds up.

misconceptions.feedback: The days passed are not changed by S. Only the ratio is.
Recall is never added to. It falls as the ratio grows.

questions.prompt: Cue A reads 12 with SD 2. Cue B reads 18 with SD 6. Weighting by 1 ÷ SD², what is the combined estimate?
hints: Find 1 ÷ SD² for each cue.
Each cue's weight is its reliability over the total.
Multiply each reading by its weight and add.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Reliabilities 1/4 and 1/36 give A a weight of (9/36)/(10/36) = 0.9. Estimate = 0.9 × 12 + 0.1 × 18 = 10.8 + 1.8 = 12.6.

questions.onCorrect: The steadier cue A carries 0.9 of the weight, so the estimate stays close to its reading.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain midpoint. The steadier cue should count for more.
That gives most of the weight to the less reliable cue.

questions.prompt: Roughly where should your best single estimate of the height land?
hints: Which of the two senses would you trust more here?
Should a trusted cue count for the same as a doubtful one?

acceptedIdeas: Closer to 50 mm than to 56 mm
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Closer to 50 mm: your eyes are the more reliable cue, so they should count for more.

choices.label: Exactly halfway, at 53 mm
Closer to 56 mm than to 50 mm
Closer to 50 mm than to 56 mm

questions.onCorrect: A steadier cue should count for more. You leaned towards sight before anyone gave you a formula.

misconceptions.feedback: The midpoint treats both cues as equally trustworthy, and they are not.
That follows the gloved fingers, which are the less reliable cue.

questions.prompt: A cue's SD doubles from 2 to 4. By what factor does its reliability, 1 ÷ SD², fall?
hints: Work out 1 ÷ SD² before and after.
The SD is squared before you take one over it.
Compare 1/4 with 1/16.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Reliability falls from 1/4 to 1/16, a factor of 4.

questions.onCorrect: SD is squared, so doubling it cuts reliability to a quarter.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the square. Doubling the SD makes SD² four times as big.
That is the fraction left. The question asks by what factor it falls.

questions.prompt: Why does the answer land nearer 30 than the midpoint, 33?
hints: Which cue has the smaller SD?

acceptedIdeas: The reading of 30 comes from the steadier cue, so it carries more weight.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The steadier cue has the bigger weight, so the estimate leans towards its reading.

choices.label: The first number always counts for more.
A smaller reading always counts for more.
The reading of 30 comes from the steadier cue, so it carries more weight.

questions.onCorrect: The estimate leans towards the steadier cue's reading, which is the one with the smaller SD.

misconceptions.feedback: Order does not matter. Only the SDs set the weights.
Size of the reading does not matter. Only reliability sets the weight.

questions.prompt: One cue has an SD of 4 mm. A second independent cue has an SD of 6 mm. What is the combined SD like?
hints: Does adding a second cue add information or remove it?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Adding any independent cue sharpens the estimate, so the combined SD is below both.

choices.label: Below 4 mm
Between 4 mm and 6 mm
Above 6 mm

questions.onCorrect: Every independent cue adds information, so the combined SD ends up below the smaller SD.

misconceptions.feedback: An average of the two would land there, but combining cues does better than an average.
Combining cues never makes an estimate worse than the best cue alone.

questions.prompt: A thief came on 10 of 20 nights. Guard A shouted on all 10 thief nights and on 9 of the 10 quiet nights. Guard B shouted on 8 of the thief nights and on 1 of the quiet nights. Which guard is better at telling a thief night from a quiet night?
hints: Look at what each guard does on the quiet nights as well.
Does shouting on every night show that a guard can tell the nights apart?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Guard B: he shouts far more often on thief nights than on quiet nights. Guard A shouts almost whatever happens.

choices.label: Guard A
Guard B
They are equally good.

questions.onCorrect: Telling nights apart means shouting far more on thief nights than on quiet ones. Guard B's two rates are far apart.

misconceptions.feedback: Guard A shouts on almost every night, thief or not. That shows willingness, not skill.
They shout at different rates on the two kinds of night. Compare each guard's two rates.

questions.prompt: A guard stays quiet on a night when a thief does come. What is that outcome called?
hints: Was a thief there, and did the guard shout or stay quiet?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A thief came and the guard stayed quiet: a miss.

questions.onCorrect: A thief was there and the guard stayed quiet, which is a miss.

misconceptions.feedback: A false alarm is a shout on a night when no thief comes.
A hit is a shout on a night when a thief does come.
A correct rejection is staying quiet on a night when no thief comes.

questions.prompt: An observer has z(H) = 1.5 and z(FA) = −0.5. What is d′?
hints: d′ subtracts the false-alarm z-score from the hit z-score.
Subtracting a negative number adds its size.
Calculate 1.5 + 0.5.
questions.onCorrect: d′ is the distance between the curves: the hit z-score minus the false-alarm z-score.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the sizes. The false-alarm z-score is negative, so subtracting it adds.
That halves the sum of the z-scores. d′ is their difference.

questions.prompt: Why does subtracting z(FA) make d′ larger here?
hints: What is subtracting a negative number the same as?

acceptedIdeas: The false-alarm z-score is below zero, so subtracting it adds its size.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Subtracting a negative number adds its size.

choices.label: The false-alarm z-score is below zero, so subtracting it adds its size.
The minus sign in the formula flips every number it meets.
d′ must always come out larger than either z-score.

questions.onCorrect: Subtracting a negative adds its size, so low false alarms raise d′.

misconceptions.feedback: Only the number after the minus sign changes. The first z-score stays as it is.
d′ is a difference, so it can be smaller than a z-score.

questions.prompt: An observer starts saying yes more readily because a miss has become costly. What has changed?
hints: Which of the two measures does cost act on?

acceptedIdeas: The criterion has moved, while sensitivity can stay the same.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Costs and rewards move the criterion. The curves have not moved, so sensitivity is the same.

choices.label: Sensitivity has fallen, because she is less careful.
The criterion has moved, while sensitivity can stay the same.
Both have changed, because they measure the same thing.

questions.onCorrect: Costs and rewards move the criterion line. The curves stay put, so d′ stays the same.

misconceptions.feedback: Saying yes more readily is not carelessness. The line moved, not the curves.
They are separate measures. One can change while the other stays the same.

questions.prompt: In Milgram's first version 26 of 40 volunteers obeyed to the end, and with the learner in the same room 16 of 40 did. By how many percentage points did obedience fall?
hints: Turn each count into a percentage.
Both conditions had 40 participants.
Subtract the same-room rate from the baseline rate.
questions.onCorrect: Compare rates, not counts: the victim's closeness cut obedience.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the baseline rate alone. Subtract the same-room rate from it.
That is the same-room rate alone. Find the gap between the two rates.

questions.prompt: On the crowded platform, how does the chance that one given person helps compare with the empty platform?
hints: More people means more chances overall. The question is about one given person.
Does a crowd change how responsible each person feels?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Lower: with many onlookers each person feels less responsible and may assume someone else will act.

choices.label: Higher
Lower
The same

questions.onCorrect: Responsibility spreads thin in a crowd. You predicted the bystander effect from everyday experience.

misconceptions.feedback: More people means more chances overall, but the question is about one given person.
A crowd changes how responsible each person feels.
