questions.prompt: In a study, 15 of 50 critical answers followed the wrong majority. What percentage is that?
hints: Divide the number that followed by the total.
The denominator is 50.
Convert 15/50 to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Conformity is the share of critical answers that followed the wrong majority.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count. Turn it into a percentage of the critical answers.
That is the share that stayed independent.

questions.prompt: In the same-room condition, 16 of 40 participants went on to the end. What percentage is that?
hints: Divide the number who continued by the number tested.
Write 16 over the group size.
Convert the fraction to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Obedience is the share who go on to the final switch.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count. Turn it into a percentage of the participants.
That is the share who stopped earlier.

questions.prompt: Two bystanders each independently act with probability 0.5. What is the probability, as a percentage, that at least one acts?
hints: Work out the chance that nobody acts.
Each person fails to act with probability 0.5.
Subtract the chance that nobody acts from 1.
questions.onCorrect: At least one acts is one minus the chance that nobody does.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one person's chance. Two people give two chances.
That is the chance that nobody acts. The question asks about at least one.

questions.prompt: A novice holds one piece per chunk and a master holds five. With a capacity of four chunks, how many more pieces can the master hold?
hints: Find how many pieces each person holds in four chunks.
The novice holds one piece in each chunk.
Subtract the novice's total from the master's.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The master holds 4 × 5 = 20 pieces, the novice 4 × 1 = 4. The difference is 16.

questions.onCorrect: Same capacity, richer chunks: four chunks of five pieces hold far more than four single pieces.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many the master holds. The question asks how many more than the novice.
That is how many the novice holds, not the difference.

questions.prompt: Why is list B so much easier to hold?
hints: Count the digits in each list.
What do you already know about the order 1 to 9?

acceptedIdeas: You know its pattern, so you hold it as one thing, not nine.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: You already know the pattern, so you hold it as one familiar unit instead of nine separate digits.

choices.label: Its digits are smaller.
It has fewer digits.
You know its pattern, so you hold it as one thing, not nine.

questions.onCorrect: Knowledge turns many items into one. You discovered chunking before it had a name.

misconceptions.feedback: Both lists have nine digits, and their size makes no difference to memory.
Both lists have nine digits. The difference is in what you already know.

questions.prompt: What is a chunk?
hints: A chunk depends on what the person knows.

acceptedIdeas: A unit that you already know
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A chunk is a unit already stored in long-term memory, whatever its size.

choices.label: Any single letter or digit
A group of exactly seven items
A unit that you already know

questions.onCorrect: A chunk is whatever you already know as a unit: a letter for one reader, a word for another.

misconceptions.feedback: A single digit is a chunk only if you know nothing that links it to others.
Chunks vary in size. The limit is on how many, not how many items.

questions.prompt: A reader knows the acronyms BBC, NHS and USA. How many chunks is the string BBCNHSUSA for this reader?
hints: Which parts of the string does the reader already know?
Each known acronym is one chunk.
Count the acronyms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: BBC, NHS and USA are three known units, so three chunks.

questions.onCorrect: Known acronyms make three chunks. Scrambled, the same letters would be nine separate chunks.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every letter. The reader holds each known acronym as one unit.
That treats the whole string as one unit. The reader knows three separate acronyms.

questions.prompt: Which part of the model directs attention among the others?
hints: Which part is a controller rather than a store?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The central executive directs attention among the other parts.

questions.onCorrect: The central executive is the controller that directs attention. The others store material.

misconceptions.feedback: The sketchpad stores images and positions. It does not direct attention.
The buffer links stored material. Directing attention is another job.

flashcards.front: Two measures correlate at r = 0.7. What percentage of their variation do they share?
Towns with more fire engines at a fire record more damage, because larger fires bring more engines and cause more damage. What is fire size in this relationship?
flashcards.back: Fire size is a confound: it drives both the number of engines and the damage.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fire size is a confound: it drives both the number of engines and the damage.

flashcards.front: A therapy group improves by 15 points and a placebo group by 9 points. How many points of improvement are due to the therapy beyond the placebo response?
What procedure gives each participant an equal chance of being placed in any condition of an experiment?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Random assignment.

flashcards.front: Two groups have means 24 and 30, both with standard deviation 12. What is Cohen's d?
Using n ≈ 16/d² per group, how many participants per group are needed to detect d = 0.8 with 80% power?
An observer's hit rate has z = 1.0 and false-alarm rate has z = −0.5. What is d′?
An observer has z(H) = 1.2 and z(FA) = −0.4. What is the criterion location c = −[z(H) + z(FA)]/2?
flashcards.back: c = −(1.2 − 0.4)/2 = −0.4, a slight bias towards yes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: c = −(1.2 − 0.4)/2 = −0.4, a slight bias towards yes.

flashcards.front: Each trial takes 700 ms and each change of task adds 250 ms. How long does the sequence ABBA take, in milliseconds?
What name is given to the phenomenon in which people counting basketball passes miss a person in a gorilla suit?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inattentional blindness.

flashcards.front: Two independent cues have standard deviations of 6 and 8. What is the standard deviation of their reliability-weighted combination?
Cue A reads 20 with SD 3 and cue B reads 30 with SD 3. What is the reliability-weighted combined estimate?
Someone groups 15 letters into 5 familiar words. Against a capacity of 4 chunks, how many chunks over the limit are they?
Which component of Baddeley and Hitch's working-memory model directs attention and coordinates the other parts?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The central executive.

flashcards.front: Using R = 1/(1 + t/9S) with stability S = 3 days, what percentage recall is predicted 9 days later?
A memory has stability 8 days, and a successful review multiplies stability by 2.5. What is the new stability in days?
Rescorla–Wagner with rate 0.4, maximum 1 and V starting at 0: what is V after two paired trials?
Which reinforcement schedule produces behaviour that is most resistant to extinction?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The variable-ratio schedule.

flashcards.front: 1,000 people are screened for a condition that 2% have. The test misses no cases but gives false positives for 5% of people without it. How many false positives are there?
A screening programme finds 12 true positives and 36 false positives. What percentage of positive results are correct?
Mould on a loaf doubles its area every day and covers the whole loaf on day 12. On which day did it cover half the loaf?
flashcards.back: Doubling means it was half the size one day earlier: day 11.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Doubling means it was half the size one day earlier: day 11.

flashcards.front: Anchors of 10 and 60 produce median estimates of 30 and 40. What is the anchoring index?
In a conformity study, 21 of 60 critical answers follow the wrong majority. What percentage conformed?
Two bystanders each independently act with probability 0.4. What is the probability, as a percentage, that at least one acts?

citations.claim: Two lists drawn as dots The clerk's lists are easier to read as a picture. Draw a sheet with the day's takings along the bottom and its rescues up the side, and put one dot for each day where its two figures meet. A day with big takings and many rescues lands far to the right and high up. A day with small takings and few rescues lands near the bottom left. In the town's picture the dots climb from the lower left to the upper right. This pattern, where two measures tend to rise and fall together, is called a correlation. Because both measures rise, it is a positive one. The second picture shows the opposite pattern. People were asked how many hours they had slept and then timed on how quickly they reacted to a light, and the dots slide downhill. Reaction time is a time, so a smaller number means a quicker person. People who slept more were quicker, so one measure falls as the other rises. That is a negative correlation. A pattern like this is easy to see but hard to describe exactly. The next screen gives a way to say how tight it is without waving a hand at the picture.

A number for the pattern A picture shows a pattern, but two people can disagree about how strong it looks. Statisticians settle that with one number, the correlation coefficient, written r. It is worked out from the dots, and it always lies between −1 and +1. Two things about r matter. Its sign gives the direction. A plus sign means the measures rise together, as in the town, where r is +0.75. A minus sign means one falls as the other rises. Its size, with the sign ignored, gives the strength. At +1 or −1 every dot sits exactly on a straight line, and at 0 there is no line to see, only a cloud. The nearer r is to either end of the scale, the more tightly the dots follow a line. Compare the two pictures. The town's dots hug a rising line, and r = +0.75. The dots for practice and test score are more spread out, and r = +0.4. Both slope upward, and the larger number marks the tighter pattern. So r tells you which way the dots lean and how closely they follow a line. It says nothing about why they lean that way, and that question is where the rest of the lesson goes.

Direction and strength are separate things. Use what the last screen said about each when you compare these two correlations. Stronger: r = −0.6 is further from zero. The minus sign only gives direction.

How much two lists share Strength can also be put another way. The kiosk's takings change from day to day, and that spread is the variation in the takings. The rescues vary too. Where two measures are correlated, part of the variation in one goes along with the variation in the other. To find out how large that part is, square r. The result is the share of the variation the two measures have in common, called the shared variation. With r = 0.4 the square is 0.4 × 0.4 = 0.16, so the two lists share 16% of their variation. The other 84% belongs to things that do not line up with the other list. Squaring also removes the sign, because a negative number times itself is positive. A correlation of −0.4 shares exactly as much as +0.4, since direction has no bearing on how much two lists have in common. A correlation that looks respectable at 0.4 still leaves most of the variation unshared.
Here are the sleep and reaction-time dots again. The first picture has a correlation of r = −0.6. Shared variance is r² = (−0.6)² = 0.36, so 36%. Squaring removes the sign.

Back to the clerk's records. Takings and rescues rise and fall together across the summer, and nobody has said why. Use what you know about a seaside town in summer. Hot weather: it brings more people to the ice-cream van and to the pool.

Something behind both lists The answer you chose is the most common reason two lists match when neither causes the other. On hot days the kiosk sells more ice cream, and on hot days the pool is crowded, so there are more swimmers and more chances for one to get into difficulty. Heat sits behind both lists and pushes them up together. A hidden variable that drives both measures like this is called a confound. You can test for a confound by holding it still. The clerk also wrote down each day's temperature, and the first picture shades every dot by it. The high-takings, high-rescue days are the hot ones. The second picture keeps only days of about the same temperature, between 21 and 23 °C. With the temperature held still, the upward lean has gone: higher takings no longer go with more rescues, and r falls from +0.75 to about 0. So the kiosk was never sending anyone into the water, because the weather drove both lists. That is why a correlation alone cannot show a cause: the dots show a pattern, but what lies behind it may be a variable nobody wrote down.
Confounds turn up wherever two measures both depend on something else, as both lists in the town depended on the weather. Age drives both measures: older children have bigger feet and better reading.

Which way the arrow points A confound is one way to explain a match, and the direction of the link is another. When exercise and mood go together, it is natural to say that exercise lifts mood, but the numbers cannot confirm that. A correlation is symmetric: swap the two axes of the picture and r stays exactly the same. The figure draws one study of exercise and mood both ways round, with r = +0.3 in each. The data look identical either way, so nothing in them says which measure is the cause. People who feel good may be the ones who go for a run. Putting the arrow the other way, from mood to exercise, is called reverse causation. Both directions can even hold at once. To separate them you would have to decide who exercises, instead of watching who chooses to. The next lesson is about doing exactly that.

Each explanation below says something different about why exercise and mood go together. Reverse causation runs the arrow from mood to exercise. Sunny weather would be a confound, and endorphins assume the original direction.

Patterns that memory builds The third way a match can arise is in the mind of the person looking. A driver says it always rains the day after he washes his car. He remembers the rainy times because they annoyed him, and he forgets the dry times, which he never gave a thought. To test his belief you have to count every day, not only the memorable ones. Say he washed the car on 10 days and it rained after 4 of them. On the other 90 days it rained after 36. The counts are different sizes, so turn each into a percentage first: 4 out of 10 is 40%, and 36 out of 90 is also 40%. Rain followed a wash no more often than it followed anything else. Believing in a link that the full counts do not show is called an illusory correlation. It grows from vivid cases, which are easy to remember. The cure is to count the dull cases too and compare rates in every group.

Hospital staff swear their emergency department is busier under a full moon. They remember the chaotic full-moon shifts. The counts for every shift are in the picture. 6/20 = 30% and 30/100 = 30%, so the difference is 0 percentage points. The remembered link is an illusory correlation.

Towns with more fire engines at a fire record more damage, because larger fires bring more engines and cause more damage. What is fire size in this relationship? Fire size is a confound: it drives both the number of engines and the damage.

Members who choose for themselves Start with the gym's own comparison. Members were free to join the programme or stay out, and the manager compared the two groups three months later. The trouble is that the groups differed long before the programme began. Someone who volunteers for a fitness programme is likely to be someone who already exercises, enjoys it and has the time. So the joiners may have been fitter on the first day, and the gap three months on may come from that head start. When people sort themselves into groups on a trait that bears on the result, the effect is called self-selection. Here the trait is how much people already exercise, and it works as a confound built into the design, much as the weather did in the seaside town. The next screen puts numbers on how large such a head start can be.

Eight members can choose. Four who exercise a lot choose the new programme, and the other four mostly stay away. Programme mean = (9 + 8 + 8 + 7)/4 = 8; other mean = (3 + 2 + 2 + 1)/4 = 2; the head start is 6 hours.

Leaving the choice to chance The repair is to take the choice away from the members. Write each name on a slip of paper, shuffle the slips and draw them. The first half go into the programme, and the rest form the control group, who carry on as before and give something to compare against. The draw does not care whether a member is keen or lazy, fit or unfit. This is random assignment: every person has the same chance of landing in either group. The figure shows one set of twelve members, each with a score for how fit they were before the study, divided up three different ways by chance. No draw makes the groups identical, and the three here differ by different amounts. What the draw guarantees is that no trait favours one group. A member who is fit, keen or short of time is as likely to be in one group as the other. That holds for traits nobody thought to measure, which is something no amount of careful choosing by researchers could promise.

Gaps that chance leaves Random assignment makes the groups fair, which is a weaker thing than making them equal. Suppose the draw puts people with fitness scores 5, 9, 4 and 6 in group A, and people with scores 7, 3, 8 and 10 in group B. Group A adds up to 24, and 24 divided by 4 gives an average of 6. Group B adds up to 28, which gives an average of 7. Group B starts one point ahead, and nothing has yet been done to either group. That gap is chance. Draw again and the gap changes, and sometimes group A will be the one in front. What matters is that the draw never leans one way: over many draws the gaps cancel out, and in larger groups each gap tends to be smaller. A small study can still be unlucky. The remedy is more people in the groups, and the draw itself stays.

Two groups were drawn at random. Group B started with an average one point above group A, before anything was done to either group. Random assignment promises fairness, not equality in one small study.

What you set and what you measure With fair groups in place, the gym still has to say exactly what it is comparing. In the study the researchers decide one thing: who gets the programme. That is the independent variable. Afterwards they measure an outcome to see whether it changed, such as each person's resting heart rate after three months. The measured outcome is the dependent variable, because its value depends on the condition. The outcome also needs a precise meaning. Fitness is a loose word, and one researcher may take it to mean strength while another means stamina. An operational definition says exactly how a concept will be measured, such as the distance a person covers in a 12-minute run. Anyone could repeat that measurement and get comparable numbers. Fixing these choices before the data arrive stops researchers from searching afterwards for some outcome that happens to differ.

Researchers assign people at random to a fitness programme or no programme. After three months they measure each person's resting heart rate. Resting heart rate is the dependent variable: it is measured to see the programme's effect.

What people expect Random groups and clear measures still leave one problem. People often improve simply because they expect to, and symptoms often fade with time anyway. If one group takes a drug and the other takes nothing, the drug group improves for three reasons mixed together: the drug, the expectation and the passing time. The fix is to give the control group an identical-looking pill with no active ingredient, called a placebo. Now both groups expect to be treated and the same time has passed. The placebo group shows how much improvement expectation and time produce on their own, so only the extra improvement in the drug group can be credited to the drug.

Who knows who got what Expectation can leak in a second way. If the people who measure the symptoms know who received the drug, their judgement can lean towards the result they hope for, often without their noticing. And if participants can tell which pill they were given, the placebo no longer keeps their expectations equal. A double-blind trial closes both gaps. Neither the participants nor the people measuring them know who received the drug until the results are in. If only one of the two parties is kept in the dark, the trial is single-blind. Together with random assignment and a placebo, double-blinding leaves the treatment as the one difference between the groups.
The control group in a drug trial gets a pill that looks the same as the real one but has no active ingredient. It keeps expectation equal, so only the active ingredient differs between the groups.

A drug trial gives one group the drug and another an identical-looking placebo. Both groups improve on a symptom score. 12 − 8 = 4 points. The placebo group shows how much improvement expectation and time alone produce.

What procedure gives each participant an equal chance of being placed in any condition of an experiment? Random assignment.

How far scores scatter Take the training course from the opening. In each class the scores are spread out, and nobody scores exactly the class average. Some do better than average and some do worse. The usual size of that scatter around the average is called the standard deviation. In class A it is about 3 points, so a typical student sits within a few points of the average. In class B it is about 30, so scores are all over the place. The standard deviation matters because a gain only means something beside it. If scores wobble by 3 points anyway, a gain of 6 is a clear shift. If they wobble by 30, a gain of 6 is about what you would see between two groups of students who had no training at all. A change should be judged against the scatter in the scores.
Both classes gained 6 points on average from the course. Think about the scatter in each class. Class A: against a spread of about 3 points, a 6-point gain is large.

Counting the gain in spreads That suggests a measure. Divide the gain by the standard deviation, and the answer says how many spreads the two groups have moved apart. In class A, 6 ÷ 3 = 2, which is two whole spreads. In class B, 6 ÷ 30 = 0.2, a fifth of a spread. This ratio is Cohen's d: the difference between two means (the averages) measured in standard deviations. The figure draws each class's scores as a bell-shaped curve, one for the untrained group and one for the trained. Where d is 2 the two curves hardly overlap, and almost every trained student beats the typical untrained one. Where d is 0.2 the curves lie nearly on top of each other. Because d counts in spreads, it lets you compare results measured in different units. Jacob Cohen suggested rough labels of 0.2 for small, 0.5 for medium and 0.8 for large, and warned that they are no substitute for knowing what counts as a worthwhile change in the field in question.
A control group scores 100 on average and a training group scores 106. Scores in both groups scatter with a standard deviation of 15. d = (106 − 100)/15 = 6/15 = 0.4.

When the two spreads differ The d we have used so far assumed both groups scatter by the same amount. Often they do not, and one group may be tightly bunched while the other is loose. Dividing by the plain average of the two spreads would treat both groups as equally important, although the looser group says more about how unreliable the scores are. The usual remedy is a pooled standard deviation. Square each group's standard deviation and average the two squares, then take the square root. Squaring makes a large spread count for far more than a small one, so the pooled value leans towards the looser group. When both spreads are equal the pooled value is just that spread, which gives a quick check on any working. Then divide the gap between the means by the pooled value, as before.

Find d for groups with means 30 and 38 and standard deviations 2 and 14. The standard deviations differ, so pool them. Square each one. 2² = 4 and 14² = 196 Average the two squares, then take the square root. This is the pooled standard deviation. √[(4 + 196) ÷ 2] = √100 = 10 Divide the difference between the means by the pooled standard deviation. (38 − 30) ÷ 10 = 0.8

The chance of finding a real effect Suppose the course really does help, with a true effect of d = 0.3. A study of a small group may still fail to show it, because a handful of students can easily be unlucky. Statistical power is the chance that a study detects an effect that is really there. A study with 80% power finds a real effect in 8 attempts out of 10. Detecting needs a rule. A result counts as significant when, if there were no real effect, a gap this large would turn up by luck fewer than 5 times in 100. That 5% cut-off is written α = 0.05, and 80% power at α = 0.05 is the usual target. Small studies have low power. They often miss real effects, and the few effects they do find tend to be lucky overestimates, because only an unusually big gap clears the cut-off in a small group.
A small study goes looking for a small effect, using a cut-off of α = 0.05. With little power, a real small effect is often missed. Those found are usually overestimates.

How many people a study needs A study can be planned to have enough power. Lehr's rule of thumb gives the number of participants needed in each group for 80% power at α = 0.05: 16 ÷ d². For a large effect with d = 0.8, that is 16 ÷ 0.64 = 25 people per group. Because d is squared, the number climbs quickly as the effect shrinks. At d = 0.5 the rule gives 16 ÷ 0.25 = 64 per group, and at d = 0.2 it gives 16 ÷ 0.04 = 400. The two pictures show why. With d = 0.5 the curves are visibly apart. With d = 0.2 they overlap so much that it takes a crowd of participants to see the gap above the scatter.
A team plans a study of an effect with d = 0.4. They want 80% power at α = 0.05. 16/0.4² = 16/0.16 = 100 per group.

A result that does not repeat A study finds an effect, and the next thing to ask is whether it holds up when someone else tries. A replication repeats the study with fresh participants. If the original effect was real, the repeat should find it again. If the original was a lucky draw from a small sample, the repeat will usually find less. The Open Science Collaboration tested this by repeating 100 psychology studies. Of the 100 originals, 97 had been significant, but the repeats reached significance in only 35 of those 97 cases. Power posing, the idea that holding an expansive pose for two minutes raises testosterone, also failed to hold up when 200 people were tested. Repeats carry most weight when they are large and preregistered, meaning the researchers published their plan, with the measures and the analysis, before collecting any data. They cannot then steer the result afterwards. A failed repeat of that kind counts for more than the original paper.

Ego depletion is the claim that self-control runs down like fuel. Published studies averaged about d = 0.6. A preregistered repeat across 23 laboratories tested 2,141 people. d = (50.4 − 50.0)/10 = 0.04, close to zero and far below the published average of about 0.6.
Ranehill and colleagues (2015) found no hormonal effect of power poses in 200 people. The other two statements are mathematical facts.

Four things that can happen on a night Take one guard on one night. Either a thief comes or none does, and either the guard shouts or stays quiet. That gives four outcomes. If a thief comes and the guard shouts, it is a hit. If a thief comes and the guard stays quiet, it is a miss. If no thief comes and the guard shouts anyway, it is a false alarm. If no thief comes and the guard stays quiet, it is a correct rejection. Two of those outcomes are mistakes, and they are different mistakes. To measure each one we divide by the nights where it could happen. The hit rate is the number of hits divided by the number of nights a thief came. The false-alarm rate is the number of false alarms divided by the number of nights no thief came. Guard A's records show how this works. A thief came on 10 nights and A shouted on every one, which is 10 hits out of 10 and a hit rate of 100%. Of the 10 quiet nights, A shouted on 9, so the false-alarm rate is 90%.
A guard is on watch on a night when a thief does come. Match what happens to one of the four outcomes. A thief came and the guard stayed quiet: a miss.

Why even a careful guard gets it wrong A quiet night is never completely quiet. A shadow moves, a gate rattles in the wind, a car door slams down the road. Call everything that is not a thief noise, and call the thief the signal. A night's overall impression is stronger when a thief is there, but the noise varies from night to night, so the impressions are not fixed. Plot how often each strength of impression occurs and you get two bell-shaped curves, one for quiet nights and one for thief nights. They overlap, because some quiet nights feel more suspicious than some thief nights. The guard has to choose a line along the scale: an impression stronger than this means shout. That line is the criterion. In the figure, the part of the thief curve to the right of the line is the share of thief nights on which the guard shouts, which is the hit rate. The part of the quiet curve to the right of the line is the false-alarm rate. Because the curves overlap, no position of the line gives all the hits and none of the false alarms.

Moving the line The guard can move the criterion without getting any better at the job. Set the line low and the guard shouts at the faintest hint. Nearly every thief night is caught, and many quiet nights are shouted at too. Set the line high and the guard shouts only at strong impressions. False alarms become rare, and some thieves slip past unchallenged. Moving the line changes both rates in the same direction, so every gain in hits is paid for with more false alarms. Look at the two pictures. The distance between the two curves is the same in both, since moving the line does not change how far apart the curves sit. That distance is set by how much stronger a thief's presence makes the impression and by how well the guard senses it. It is the measure of skill, and the line is not. The next screens turn it into a number.

Over twenty nights a thief came on ten of them. Think about the line each guard has set and about how often each one shouts on each kind of night. Guard B: he shouts far more often on thief nights than on quiet nights. Guard A shouts almost whatever happens.

A number for skill The distance between the curves is called d′ (say d-prime), or sensitivity. We cannot see the curves, only the rates, so we turn each rate into a z-score. A z-score says how many standard deviations a position sits above the middle of its curve. The table is standard: a rate of 0.50 gives z = 0, 0.80 gives 0.84, 0.90 gives 1.28 and 0.954 gives 1.68. A rate below one half gives the same size with a minus sign, so 0.20 gives −0.84, 0.10 gives −1.28 and 0.07 gives −1.48. Then d′ = z(H) − z(FA), where H is the hit rate and FA the false-alarm rate. Guard B shouted on 8 of 10 thief nights, so H = 0.80 and z(H) = 0.84. B shouted on 1 of 10 quiet nights, so FA = 0.10 and z(FA) = −1.28. Subtracting a negative adds its size, so d′ = 0.84 − (−1.28) = 2.12. A large d′ belongs to a guard who catches most thieves and rarely raises a false alarm. If the shouting ignores what is actually happening, d′ is near zero, even when many thieves get caught.

Another guard has a hit rate of 0.80 and a false-alarm rate of 0.20. The table on the last screen gives their z-scores. d′ = z(H) − z(FA) = 0.84 − (−0.84) = 1.68.

How ready to say yes Skill is half the story. The other half is where the guard puts the line, and that is measured by the criterion, written c. It is found from the same two z-scores: c = −[z(H) + z(FA)] ÷ 2. If c is 0 the line sits midway between the two curves. A negative c means the line sits low and the guard says yes readily. A positive c means the line sits high and the guard is cautious. For Guard B, z(H) = 0.84 and z(FA) = −1.28, so the sum is −0.44. Halving it gives −0.22, and the minus sign in front turns that into c = +0.22. Guard B leans very slightly towards caution. The two measures answer different questions. Training and practice raise d′. Costs and rewards move c: a guard who is blamed for every missed thief will lower the line, and one who is blamed for waking the street will raise it.
A guard starts shouting more readily because missing a thief has become costly. Costs and rewards move the criterion. The curves have not moved, so sensitivity is the same.

Attention is selective Start with something you have probably done. You are reading in a café when someone at the next table begins an interesting story, and a minute later you realise you have read the same line three times. Your senses were taking in the page the whole time. Your attention was somewhere else. At every moment your senses take in far more than the mind can use. Attention is how it chooses. It follows one stream, such as the story at the next table or the line you are reading, and turns the others down. This is selective attention, and it is what lets you follow one voice in a noisy room. The choice has a price. What you are not attending to is dealt with far less thoroughly than what you are attending to. How far that can go is shown by an experiment that has been repeated many times.

The gorilla in the game In the experiment, viewers watched a short film of two teams passing basketballs, one team in white shirts and one in black. They were asked to count the passes made by the white team. Partway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the middle of the players, thumped their chest and walked out again. The gorilla was on screen for several seconds. When viewers were asked afterwards whether they had noticed anything unusual, around half had not seen the gorilla at all. They were not careless or short-sighted. Many had counted the passes accurately. Their attention was on the white shirts and the ball, and an object in plain view, which they did not expect and were not looking for, never registered. This is inattentional blindness: failing to notice a clearly visible, unexpected object because attention is directed at something else. Looking at a thing and seeing it are different, and attention is what links the two.
Here is a class demonstration with the same film. The counts show how many of the people counting passes missed the gorilla. 14/30 = 0.4667, or 46.7%, close to the 46% Simons and Chabris reported.

The price of changing job Now return to the eight cards. Call the sums task A, in which you judge whether a digit is odd or even, and the word puzzles task B, in which you judge whether a letter is a vowel or a consonant. Every trial takes some time. When you move from A to B, or from B to A, the mind has to drop one set of rules and pick up the other, and that takes extra time called the switch cost. Repeating the same task has no such cost. To count the switches in a sequence, look at each pair of neighbouring trials and count the pairs where the task changes. The first trial is not a switch, because nothing came before it. AAB has one switch, between the second A and the B. ABAB has three. The total time for a sequence is the number of trials times the time per trial, plus the number of switches times the switch cost. The figure shows two orders of eight trials with the same trial time and the same switch cost. The alternating order has a switch between every pair of neighbouring trials. The blocked order has just one, in the middle. Both orders contain the same work, and the difference in time comes entirely from the switches.
Read a sequence from left to right and compare each trial with the one before it. A to B, then B to A: two switches. B to B is not a switch.

Now use the digit and letter judgements from the cards. Each trial takes 600 ms, and each change of task adds 200 ms. ABABABAB has 7 switches: 8 × 600 + 7 × 200 = 6,200 ms.

Blocks against alternating The two orders of the eight cards have the same number of trials, so the time spent on the cards themselves is the same. Only the number of switches differs. Doing the sums first and the words after, in the order AAAABBBB, has a single switch. Alternating has one between every pair of neighbouring trials, and each of those switches adds the same cost. People can reduce a switch cost by getting ready. If you know which task comes next, you switch faster. Preparation shrinks the cost without removing it, which is why answering messages while writing a report takes longer than it feels. Each message is a switch away from the report, and the return to the report is another.
Each trial takes 600 ms and each change of task adds 200 ms. Both orders contain eight trials. ABABABAB has 7 switches and AAAABBBB has 1; the extra 6 switches cost 6 × 200 = 1,200 ms.

Two things at once The same cost appears outside the laboratory. Driving is a task, and so is working through a problem in your head. A driver who does both is not doing them at the same instant. Attention moves between them, and each move is a switch. Watson and Strayer asked whether anyone escapes this. They put 200 people in a driving simulator and gave them a demanding memory-and-arithmetic task to do while they drove. They then checked whether either task got worse compared with doing it alone. For nearly everyone it did. A very small group, whom the researchers called supertaskers, showed no measurable cost on either task. Because supertaskers are so rare, a person who feels sure they multitask well is much more likely to be one of the others.
Some drivers in the study showed no cost at all from doing a second demanding task. The counts are in the picture. 5/200 = 0.025, or 2.5%.

One sense gives a wobbly reading Start with sight alone. You look at the block and your eyes give you a number, say 50 mm. Look again after blinking and you get 49, and the next look gives 52. The readings gather around the true height, yet no single look is exact. Over many looks they average out near 50 mm and typically stray from that average by about 2 mm. That typical stray is the standard deviation, or SD, the usual size of a scatter around an average. A small SD means the readings bunch tightly, so one look is nearly as good as any other. A large SD means they are scattered, so any one look could be well off. Every source of information about the world wobbles in this way and has an SD of its own. Psychologists call such a source a cue. Sight is a cue to the block's height. Touch is another. Because no cue is exact, working out the height is a matter of inference: a best guess drawn from the evidence you have.

Two senses that disagree Now put on the thick gloves and feel the block. Your fingers say 56 mm. Gloves dull the sense of touch, so these readings wobble more than the ones from your eyes, with an SD of 4 mm against sight's 2 mm. You are left with two readings, 50 mm and 56 mm, which cannot both be exact. One way out is to split the difference and say 53 mm. That treats the two cues as equally good, and whether they are is the real question. Think of two friends giving you directions. One has lived in the area for years and the other visited once. If they disagree you would not give them equal say. You would lean towards the friend whose directions have turned out right more often, while still listening to the other. The mind faces the same choice with every pair of senses, and it makes it with a rule that can be written down.

Weighing cues by how steady they are The steadier cue should count for more, and there is a precise way to say how much more. Give each cue a number for how far it can be trusted, called its reliability, and set it to 1 ÷ SD², where SD² means the SD multiplied by itself. A cue with an SD of 1 mm has a reliability of 1 ÷ (1 × 1) = 1. A cue with an SD of 3 mm has a reliability of 1 ÷ (3 × 3) = 1/9. Because the SD is multiplied by itself, a cue that wobbles more loses reliability quickly. Each cue's weight is its share of the total. Add the reliabilities, then divide each cue's reliability by that total, so that the weights add up to 1. The combined estimate is the weighted average: multiply each reading by its weight and add the results. The figure shows a second, shorter block. Sight reads 30 mm with an SD of 1 mm, and touch reads 36 mm with an SD of 3 mm. The taller, narrower curve belongs to the steadier cue. The combined estimate, marked in teal, sits close to the sight reading. If both cues were equally steady they would get equal weights, and the estimate would fall exactly halfway between them. The midpoint is a special case, correct only when the cues are matched.

For a second, shorter block, sight reads 30 mm (SD 1 mm) and touch reads 36 mm (SD 3 mm). Find the combined estimate. Find each cue's reliability, 1 ÷ SD². 1 ÷ 1 = 1 and 1 ÷ 9 = 1/9 Divide each by the total, 1 + 1/9 = 10/9, to get the weights. 1 ÷ (10/9) = 0.9 and (1/9) ÷ (10/9) = 0.1 Weight the readings and add them. 0.9 × 30 + 0.1 × 36 = 27 + 3.6 = 30.6 Read the result: 30.6 mm sits well below the midpoint of 33 mm, close to the steadier cue.

Two cues are sharper than one The combined estimate has a second advantage over each cue taken alone: it wobbles less. Two witnesses who each saw part of an event give a better account together than the better witness gives alone, because each fills in what the other left uncertain. The SD of the combined estimate follows from the reliabilities. Add the two reliabilities and take the square root of the total. The combined SD is 1 divided by that root. Written out, it is 1 ÷ √(1/SD₁² + 1/SD₂²). Take two cues with SDs of 5 mm and 12 mm. Their reliabilities are 1/25 and 1/144, which add up to 169/3600. The square root of that is 13/60, and 1 divided by 13/60 is 60/13, about 4.6 mm. That is smaller than both 5 and 12. In the figure the narrow teal curve is the combined estimate. It is taller and thinner than either cue's own curve, so using both senses pins the height down more tightly than the better sense could by itself. Even a poor cue helps, as long as its errors are unrelated to the other cue's errors.

Two cues give independent readings of the same block. One has an SD of 3 mm and the other an SD of 4 mm. Use the formula for the combined SD. What is the standard deviation of the combined estimate, in millimetres? 1/9 + 1/16 = 25/144; the combined SD is √(144/25) = 12/5 = 2.4 mm.

What you expect is evidence too So far every cue has come through a sense. A third source of evidence needs no sense at all: what you already expect to see. Suppose a line flashes up for an instant and you cannot make out its tilt. If you expect it to be upright, that expectation pulls what you see towards upright. The mind treats the expectation like one more cue. It has a reading, such as a tilt of 0° for an upright line, and an SD that says how firmly the expectation is held. Expectations built over many years are firm, so their SD is small and they carry a large weight whenever the glimpse is poor. An expectation used this way is called a prior, because it is in place before the new evidence arrives. Perception shaped by what you know and expect, instead of being built only from the incoming signal, is top-down processing. In the figure, a line is expected to be upright (0°, SD 2°) and the glimpse says 8° (SD 4°). The combined tilt stays close to upright. A hollow mask seen from the inside shows the same thing at a larger scale. Its surface is dented inwards, yet it looks like an ordinary face bulging outwards, because the expectation that faces bulge is so firm that it outweighs the shading that says otherwise.

Holding things in mind for a few seconds While you waited those ten seconds, something kept the digits available. Psychologists call it working memory: the small mental workspace that holds a few pieces of information for a short time while you use them. It is what lets you keep a phone number in mind while you walk across the room to dial it, or hold the start of a sentence while the end of it arrives. Working memory differs from long-term memory, which holds your knowledge for years and has room for an enormous amount. Working memory is small and easily overwritten. If someone asks you a question before you reach the keypad, the number is often gone. The size of the store was first estimated in 1956, when the psychologist George Miller gathered results from many experiments and concluded that people can hold about seven items at once, give or take two. That became one of the best-known numbers in psychology, yet it leaves the two lists unexplained. If the limit were seven items, list B would break it as badly as list A does. Something else must set the limit.

What counts as one piece The answer turns on what an item is. Later work, notably by the psychologist Nelson Cowan in 2001, looked at what people can hold when they have no chance to repeat the items to themselves or to group them. The limit came out at about four, and the unit being counted is the chunk. A chunk is a unit you already know as one thing. Someone who has never met the letters R, A and F together sees three separate letters, which make three chunks. A British reader knows RAF as the air force, so for that reader the same letters make a single chunk. The amount of memory used depends on what you know. Now return to the two lists. List B runs 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9, a run you know so well that it behaves as one chunk. List A follows no pattern you know, so each digit is a chunk of its own. Nine chunks is more than the store can hold. The figure shows the same idea with an eleven-digit phone number. Read as eleven separate digits, the number is far over the limit. Read as groups of five, three and three, it makes three chunks and fits with room to spare. The capacity is the same in both pictures. Only the number of chunks needed has changed.

Nine unrelated digits are read once, with no way to group them. Each digit is its own chunk, and the capacity is four chunks. How many digits exceed the limit? Nine chunks against a capacity of four leaves 9 − 4 = 5 beyond the limit.

Making chunks bigger If the limit is on chunks, and a chunk is whatever you know as one unit, there is a way to fit more into the same space: make each chunk carry more. This is chunking, the grouping of items into units you already know. A reader who knows the acronyms CD and TV sees the four letters CDTV as two chunks. Scramble them into DCVT and each letter becomes a chunk of its own, four in all. The limit of about four chunks is the same for everyone. What differs is how much each chunk contains. Four single-letter chunks hold four letters. Four chunks that are each a three-letter acronym hold twelve. Card numbers and postcodes are written in groups for this reason. The groups split a long string into pieces small enough to carry, and people who learn the groups well can carry them without effort.

How a chess master remembers a board Chunking is easiest to see in experts. In the early 1970s William Chase and Herbert Simon showed a chess master and some weaker players a real game position for five seconds, then asked each of them to rebuild it from memory. The master put back far more of the pieces. It would be easy to guess that masters simply have better memories. A second condition says otherwise. When the pieces were placed at random, as they never would be in a game, the master's advantage mostly disappeared. A master has seen so many real positions that a cluster of pieces, such as a castled king with the three pawns in front of it, is one familiar pattern. A weaker player sees the same cluster as separate pieces. With random placements the patterns are gone, and the master has nothing to chunk. So the master's working memory is ordinary, with the same limit of about four chunks. The difference lies in how much each chunk holds. The figure shows a simplified position of twelve pieces. The master sees the twelve pieces as three patterns, which fit in a store of four chunks. The novice sees twelve single pieces, which overflow it.

Working memory has parts So far working memory has been a single store with a size. In 1974 the psychologists Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch argued that it is better described as a small team of parts, each handling a different kind of material, with a controller above them. The model has been revised since, but its main parts have held up. The phonological loop holds sounds and words. It is the voice in your head that repeats a phone number to keep it alive. The visuospatial sketchpad holds images and positions, such as the layout of a room or the route you are about to walk. The episodic buffer ties material from these parts and from long-term memory into one scene or story. Above them sits the central executive, which stores nothing itself. It directs attention and decides what to hold and what to drop. Separate parts explain something a single store cannot. Two jobs that use different parts, such as remembering a phone number and picturing a route, interfere with each other very little. Two jobs that use the same part, such as holding two phone numbers at once, interfere a great deal.

Each part of the model has its own job, and one of them does not hold material at all. Which part of the model directs attention among the others? The central executive directs attention among the other parts.

Forgetting is fast, then slow Return to the 100 words. You lost 40 in the first day, and the 60 that remain are the ones that stuck best, so they go more slowly. Say 10 more go over the following week and a few more over the month after. Draw a graph of how much you can recall against the time since you learned the words, and the result is a curve that falls steeply at first and then flattens. Hermann Ebbinghaus found this shape in the 1880s. He learned lists of nonsense syllables and tested himself after different delays. In 2015 Jaap Murre and Joeri Dros repeated the experiment with one volunteer and got a curve of the same shape, so the pattern has held up for well over a century. The curve describes memory in general, and it does not fit every memory equally well. Some memories are strong and fall along a flat curve. Others are fragile and drop quickly. To make use of the curve we need a number that says which kind of memory we have.

A number for how long a memory lasts The number is called stability, written S. It is the number of days until the chance of recalling the memory has fallen to 90%. A memory with a stability of 3 days is still 90% likely to come back after 3 days. A memory with a stability of 30 days takes ten times as long to reach that point. With S in hand, one formula gives the predicted recall R after t days: R = 1 ÷ (1 + t ÷ 9S). Here 9S means 9 × S. At t = 0 the fraction is zero and R = 1 ÷ 1 = 100%. As t grows the fraction grows and R falls, steeply at first and then more slowly, which is the curve Ebbinghaus found. Put t = S and the fraction is 1/9, so R = 1 ÷ (1 + 1/9) = 0.9, which matches the definition of S. Take S = 3 days and look at day 18. Then 9S = 27 and t ÷ 9S = 18 ÷ 27 = 2/3. That gives R = 1 ÷ (1 + 2/3) = 3/5, which is 60%. The figure draws the whole curve for a memory with a stability of 3 days. Press play and watch recall fall. Stability sits under the fraction, so a larger S makes t ÷ 9S grow more slowly and the curve flatter. A memory with a large stability fades slowly, and one with a small stability fades fast.

What a review does to a memory So far the memory has been left alone. Now suppose you test yourself on the words on day 4 and recall them correctly. A successful recall does two things. It lifts recall back to nearly 100%, as if the clock had restarted, and it raises the memory's stability, so the curve that follows is flatter than the one before. Each success multiplies the stability by some factor. If a review multiplies it by 2.5, a memory with S = 2 days becomes one with S = 5 days, and forgetting from then on is two and a half times as slow. This is why reviews can be spaced further and further apart. The second review can wait longer than the first, and the third longer still. Reviewing at widening gaps is called spaced practice, also known as distributed practice. The opposite is massed practice, which crams all the study into one session. The figure compares a memory reviewed on day 3 with one that is left alone. The reviewed memory is back near 100% on day 3 and then declines far more slowly than the other. By the end of the month the gap between them is large, even though the reviewed memory cost only one short test.

citations.claim: Testing yourself beats rereading There is one more choice to make about a review, which is how to do it. You can reread your notes, which feels smooth and familiar. Or you can close them and try to recall what they said, which feels harder and more uncertain. The second method is called retrieval practice, and it is the kind of review the stability story assumed, since a review there means a successful act of recall. Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke compared the two in 2006. Students studied a passage and then either reread it or practised recalling it. Five minutes later the rereaders did better, recalling 81% of the ideas in the passage against 75%. If the test had stopped there, rereading would have looked like the better method. The students were tested again a week later and the order reversed. Those who had practised recalling kept far more than those who had reread. Effortful recall feels worse at the time and lasts longer, so the feeling that rereading is going well is a poor guide to what will last. This is why good flashcard systems make you try to answer before they show you the card.

The dog and the bell In the 1890s the Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov was studying digestion in dogs when he noticed that they began to drool before any food reached them, at the sight of the person who usually brought it. He turned that observation into an experiment. Food makes a hungry dog drool without any training, and a bell makes it prick up its ears and do little else. Pavlov rang the bell just before the food arrived, again and again. After enough of these pairings the dog drooled at the bell alone. The bell had become a conditioned stimulus, a signal that has gained its power through experience, and drooling at it was learned. Learning in which a signal comes to predict an outcome through repeated pairing is called classical conditioning. The pairing matters. A bell that rings at random times, with no link to the food, teaches the dog nothing, because the bell tells it nothing about what comes next. That leaves a question about pace. The first pairing is the biggest surprise to the dog and later ones surprise it less, and a simple rule describes how the learning grows.

How much each pairing teaches In 1972 Robert Rescorla and Allan Wagner proposed that rule. Call the strength of the link between bell and food V, the associative strength. It starts at 0 and can rise towards a maximum, written λ (the Greek letter lambda), which is the most the food can support. With food present, λ = 1. Each pairing closes a share of the gap between V and λ. The rule is ΔV = rate × (λ − V), where ΔV is the change in V on that trial and the rate says how quickly the animal learns, a number between 0 and 1. Take a rate of 0.25. On the first pairing V is 0, so the gap is 1 and V rises by 0.25 × 1 = 0.25. On the second pairing the gap is 1 − 0.25 = 0.75, so V rises by 0.25 × 0.75 = 0.1875 and reaches 0.4375. The figure shows six pairings. Each step is smaller than the one before, because less of the gap is left to close. The first pairing teaches the most and the tenth teaches very little. That fits the dog that is quick to start drooling and then settles into a steady response.

When the food stops coming Suppose the bell keeps ringing after the food has been taken away. The same rule applies, with one change. With no food the most the bell can predict is 0, so λ = 0. If V stands at 0.8 and the rate is 0.25, the gap λ − V is −0.8, which is negative, so V moves down by 0.25 × 0.8 = 0.2 to 0.6. A bell that no longer predicts food loses its power, trial by trial. This fading response is called extinction. Extinction does not wipe the dog's learning clean. If the bell is rung again after a rest, the drooling often returns for a while, which is called spontaneous recovery. It looks as though extinction adds a second piece of learning, that the bell no longer means food, on top of the first and leaves the first in place. The simple rule treats extinction as unlearning, so it is a good first model and an incomplete one.

Learning from consequences The dog has so far learned from what comes before an event: the bell. Now ask what happens to an action that is followed by something. Teach the dog to sit by giving it a treat each time it sits, and it sits more often. Sitting was followed by a consequence, and the consequence changed how likely the behaviour is. This is operant conditioning, studied by B. F. Skinner and, before him, by Edward Thorndike. Two choices describe any consequence. It either adds something or takes something away, and psychologists call these positive and negative, words that only mean added and removed. It also either makes the behaviour more likely, which is reinforcement, or less likely, which is punishment. The treat for sitting adds something pleasant and sitting rises, so it is positive reinforcement. A car's seat-belt alarm stops once the belt is fastened, so removing an unpleasant sound makes fastening more likely, which is negative reinforcement. A library fine takes money away and late returns fall, which is negative punishment. Touching a hot hob adds pain and the touching falls, which is positive punishment.

Decide whether something was added or removed, and whether the behaviour rose or fell. Praise follows a pupil raising a hand, and hand-raising becomes more frequent. Is this positive or negative reinforcement? Positive reinforcement: praise is added and the behaviour rises.

How often the rewards arrive A trainer must also decide how often to give the treat. The rule for when a reward is given is a schedule of reinforcement. Some schedules depend on how many responses the animal makes, and some depend on how much time has passed. A fixed-ratio schedule gives a reward after a set number of responses, such as every fourth peck. Under a variable-ratio schedule the number changes unpredictably around an average, so the reward might follow 2 pecks, then 7, then 3. A fixed-interval schedule rewards the first response after a set time has passed, so the reward lands on a response and responses during the wait earn nothing. A variable-interval schedule makes the wait unpredictable. The figure records responses over time for a fixed ratio of 4 and a variable ratio that averages 4. The two pay out about equally often, but they differ in what happens when the rewards stop. On a fixed schedule the animal soon sees that the pattern has broken and gives up. On a variable-ratio schedule it cannot tell a long gap from the end of the rewards, so it keeps responding for far longer. An angler whose fish bite after an unpredictable number of casts knows the effect.

A pigeon pecks a key on a fixed-ratio 5 schedule: every fifth peck is rewarded. A pigeon on a fixed-ratio 5 schedule makes 30 pecks. How many rewards does it earn? Every fifth response is rewarded: 30/5 = 6.

A rat is on a fixed-interval schedule with a wait of 10 seconds. Only a press can earn the reward. On a fixed-interval 10-second schedule, a rat presses every 3 seconds for 60 seconds. The first press at least 10 s after the previous reward is rewarded. How many rewards does it earn? Rewarded presses fall at 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 s: five rewards.
A slot machine pays out after an unpredictable number of plays, averaging one win in twenty. Which reinforcement schedule is this? Variable ratio: rewards follow an unpredictable number of responses.

A child's screen time is taken away after they hit a sibling, and the hitting becomes less frequent. Which consequence is this? Something pleasant is removed (negative) and the behaviour decreases (punishment).

What is V after two pairings? Trial 1: V = 0 + 0.3 × 1 = 0.3. Trial 2: V = 0.3 + 0.3 × (1 − 0.3) = 0.51.
Why does V fall on a bell-alone trial? Without food the bell predicts nothing, so the maximum is 0 and the change is negative.
Starting from V = 0, what is the final V? Pairings: 0.5, then 0.75. Alone: 0.75 + 0.5 × (0 − 0.75) = 0.375.
Praise follows a pupil raising a hand, and hand-raising becomes more frequent. Is this positive or negative reinforcement? Positive reinforcement: praise is added and the behaviour rises.
It makes 30 pecks. How many rewards does it earn? Every fifth response is rewarded: 30/5 = 6.

On a fixed-interval 10-second schedule, a rat presses every 3 seconds for 60 seconds. The first press at least 10 s after the previous reward is rewarded. How many rewards does it earn? Rewarded presses fall at 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 s: five rewards.
Rescorla–Wagner with rate 0.4, maximum 1 and V starting at 0: what is V after two paired trials? 0.4, then 0.4 + 0.4 × 0.6 = 0.64.
Which reinforcement schedule produces behaviour that is most resistant to extinction? The variable-ratio schedule.

Counting the beeps Go back to the airport and count. Among the 1,000 bags, 2 hold a banned item and the scanner beeps for both. Of the other 998 it beeps for 98. In total the scanner beeps for 2 + 98 = 100 bags. A bag that has beeped is one of those 100, and only 2 of them hold anything banned. A beep means a banned item about 2 times in 100. That answer came from counting bags. No percentages had to be multiplied. Picturing a crowd of real things and counting them is a method known as natural frequencies, and it makes problems of this kind much easier. Percentages describe a group but hide the individuals in it. Once a percentage is turned into a number of people, the arithmetic is only counting. Here is the move in general. Suppose 2% of a group of 1,000 people have a condition. Two per cent of 1,000 is 20 people. If a test catches half of them, that is 10 people. Each step takes a percentage of a group and turns it into a head count, and the next step works from that count.

Screening a thousand people Now take a medical screening test. The condition is present in 2% of 1,000 people, and the share of a group who have a condition is called the base rate, here 2%. The test is imperfect. It flags half of the people who have the condition, which is its hit rate, and it also flags 5% of the people who do not, its false-alarm rate. Counting gives the whole picture. Two per cent of 1,000 is 20 people with the condition, and half of them, 10 people, are flagged. These are the true positives: people with the condition whom the test flags. The other 980 people are healthy, and 5% of 980 is 49 people flagged by mistake. These are the false positives: healthy people whom the test flags. The figure draws the 1,000 people in this way. The false positives outnumber the true positives by almost five to one, although the test catches half of the people who have the condition and wrongly flags only one healthy person in twenty. The healthy group is so much larger than the group with the condition that even a small error rate produces many flags.

1,000 people are screened for a disease that 1% have. The test flags 90% of those who have it, so there are 9 true positives. It also wrongly flags 10% of people who do not have the disease. How many false positives are there? 1,000 − 10 = 990 people do not have the disease; 10% of 990 = 99 false positives.

The tempting answer Most people, shown a result like this, answer with the test's hit rate. A test that catches 90% of cases seems to mean that a positive result is 90% likely to be right. The accuracy of the test is vivid and the rarity of the condition is easy to overlook, so the vivid number wins. Ignoring how common something is when judging a single case is called base-rate neglect. The mistake shows up outside medicine too. Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described a man called Steve, who is shy and tidy and loves order. They asked people whether he is more likely to be a librarian or a farmer. People chose librarian because the description sounds like one. But farmers vastly outnumber librarians, and that fact is evidence as well. People let the description crowd it out. The next screen gives a way to avoid the mistake. It puts both numbers, how rare the condition is and how good the test is, into a single count.

Who the positive result is about A person who has just tested positive belongs to one particular group, the people the test flagged. That group is made up of the true positives and the false positives together. The chance that this person has the condition is the share of the flagged group who really do. The calculation is true positives ÷ (true positives + false positives). Go back to the 1,000 people screened with a base rate of 2%. There were 10 true positives and 49 false positives. That makes 59 flagged people, and 10 ÷ 59 is about 0.17. A positive result there gives about a 17% chance of having the condition, far below the 50% that the hit rate might suggest. Dividing by the 20 people who have the condition would answer a different question, which is how likely a person with the condition is to be flagged. That is the hit rate again. A positive result is a fact about the flagged group, so the flagged group is the number to divide by.

500 people are tested and 10% have the disease. The test flags 60% of cases and 20% of healthy people. Find the share of positives that are right. Split the people into those with and without the disease. 10% of 500 = 50, so 450 do not Count the true positives and the false positives. 60% of 50 = 30 and 20% of 450 = 90 Divide the true positives by all positives. 30 ÷ (30 + 90) = 30 ÷ 120 = 25%

Of 1,000 people, 9 true positives and 99 false positives test positive. A person is among the flagged. What is the probability, as a percentage, that a person who tests positive has the disease? Give one decimal place. 9/(9 + 99) = 9/108 = 0.0833, or 8.3%.

The same test in a different crowd The test was never the whole problem. Its hit rate and false-alarm rate describe how it behaves on people who have the condition and on people who do not. What a positive result means also depends on the mix of people being tested. Move the same test into a clinic where patients have been sent because of symptoms, and the mix changes. Suppose 20% of the 1,000 people tested at the clinic have the condition, and the test is as before: it flags half of them and 5% of the healthy. Now 200 people have the condition and 100 of them are flagged. Of the 800 healthy people, 40 are flagged. The flagged group holds 140 people and 100 of them have the condition, which is about 71%. Compare that with 17% when only 2% were affected. The figure sets the two crowds side by side. Nothing about the test changed between the two, yet a positive result means more than four times as much in the clinic. The meaning of a result depends on who is being tested, which is why a test given to everyone and a test given to people with symptoms have to be judged differently.

Use the same test, with a 90% hit rate and a 10% false-alarm rate, in a clinic where 10% of 1,000 people have the disease. What percentage of positive results are true positives? 100 have it and 90 test positive; 900 do not and 90 test positive; 90/180 = 50%.

A witness who names colours correctly 75% of the time says the cab was blue. What is the probability, as a percentage, that it was blue? Give one decimal place. Per 1,000 cabs: 150 blue cabs called blue and 200 green cabs called blue; 150/350 = 42.9%.

A screening programme finds 12 true positives and 36 false positives. What percentage of positive results are correct? 12/(12 + 36) = 12/48 = 25%.

An anchor is a number met before a judgement that pulls the judgement towards itself. Tversky and Kahneman's rigged wheel stopped at 10 or 65 before volunteers estimated the share of UN members that are African countries. The median is the middle guess. Anchoring bias is the pull of a starting number that carries no information.
After the wheel stopped on 10 the median estimate was 25%, and after 65 it was 45%, a gap of 20 percentage points from a plainly irrelevant number.

The anchoring index is the gap between median estimates divided by the gap between anchors. 0 means the anchors were ignored and 1 means estimates moved as far as the anchors. Anchors 0 and 100 with medians 30 and 50 give 0.2. The wheel study gives 20 ÷ 55, about 0.36.
Anchors of 10 and 70 with medians of 30 and 51 give an anchoring index of 21 ÷ 60 = 0.35.
Anchors of 20 and 80 with median oak-age estimates of 35 and 59 years give an index of 24 ÷ 60 = 0.4.

The availability heuristic judges how common something is by how easily examples come to mind. It misleads when memorable events are not frequent. Words with k as the third letter are about twice as common as words starting with k.
In a sample of 600 words containing k, 200 start with k, which is 33.3%; words with k third are twice as common though harder to recall.

Kahneman's System 1 is fast, effortless thinking and System 2 is slower, deliberate checking; they are names for ways of thinking, not brain organs. A quick answer to a cap-and-scarf style problem can fail a check that sets up 2x + 4 = 6.
A bat and a ball cost £1.10 and the bat costs £1.00 more. The quick answer of 10p would make the total £1.20, and the ball costs 5p.
Anchors of 100 and 500 produce median estimates of 220 and 340. What is the anchoring index? (340 − 220)/(500 − 100) = 120/400 = 0.3.

After several news reports of shark attacks, a swimmer judges sharks a bigger risk than drowning. Judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind is which heuristic? The availability heuristic: vivid, easily recalled cases feel common.
A pen and a notebook cost £2.20 together. The notebook costs £2.00 more than the pen. How much does the pen cost, in pence? Pen x, notebook x + 200: 2x + 200 = 220, so x = 10p.
By how many percentage points did the medians differ? 45 − 25 = 20 percentage points.
What does an index of 0.35 say about the anchors? An index between 0 and 1 shows how far the estimates moved, as a share of the anchors' gap.
What is the anchoring index, (difference in medians) ÷ (difference in anchors)? (59 − 35)/(80 − 20) = 24/60 = 0.4.

In a sample of 600 English words containing k, 200 start with k and 400 have k as the third letter. What percentage start with k? Give one decimal place. 200/600 = 0.333, or 33.3%: words with k third are twice as common, though harder to recall.
How much does the ball cost, in pence? Ball x, bat x + 100p: 2x + 100 = 110, so x = 5p. The intuitive 10p would make the total £1.20.
Mould on a loaf doubles its area every day and covers the whole loaf on day 12. On which day did it cover half the loaf? Doubling means it was half the size one day earlier: day 11.
Anchors of 10 and 60 produce median estimates of 30 and 40. What is the anchoring index? (40 − 30)/(60 − 10) = 10/50 = 0.2.

In Asch's line-judgement studies, confederates gave a unanimous wrong answer on critical trials. Alone, people erred on under 1% of judgements. About 37% of critical answers and about 75% of people conformed at least once. Conformity rate is conforming critical answers divided by all critical answers.
In a replication, 18 people gave 12 critical answers each, and 72 of the 216 followed the wrong majority, 33.3%.

In Milgram's 1963 study, volunteers were told to shock a learner for errors up to 450 volts under an experimenter's instruction. The learner was an actor and no shocks were real. Obedience is measured by the share who went to the final switch.
In Milgram's baseline condition 26 of 40 volunteers went to 450 volts, which is 65%.
Obedience fell as the learner came closer: 26 of 40 with the learner in another room, 16 of 40 in the same room and 12 of 40 with the hand on the plate. Rates are compared in percentage points.
Obedience fell from 65% to 30% between the baseline and touch-proximity conditions, 35 percentage points.

Burger's 2009 partial replication stopped at 150 volts and found 70% willing to continue, against 82.5% in Milgram's comparable condition. Perry's archive work found that experimenters sometimes left the script and many participants doubted the shocks.

Darley and Latané's intercom seizure study found 85% helped when they thought they alone heard it and 31% when they thought four others heard. Diffusion of responsibility lowers each person's chance of acting.
If n people act independently with chance p, at least one acts with chance 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ; three people at 0.3 give 65.7%.
Two independent bystanders each acting with probability 0.5 give a 75% chance that at least one acts.
The 38 silent witnesses to the Genovese murder is largely a myth. Philpot and colleagues' CCTV study of 219 real conflicts found someone intervened in 91%, more often with more bystanders.
Five independent bystanders each acting with probability 0.2 give 1 − 0.8⁵ = 67.2% that at least one acts.
Three bystanders each independently help with probability 0.5. What is the probability, as a percentage, that at least one helps? P(nobody) = 0.5³ = 0.125; P(at least one) = 0.875, or 87.5%.
Which statement fits the evidence from CCTV recordings of real public conflicts? Philpot and colleagues (2020) found intervention in 91% of 219 conflicts, rising with the number of bystanders.

Milgram's baseline had 26 of 40 obeying to the end; the same-room condition had 16 of 40. By how many percentage points did obedience fall? 26/40 = 65% and 16/40 = 40%; 65 − 40 = 25 percentage points.
What percentage of critical answers conformed? Give one decimal place. 18 × 12 = 216 critical answers; 72/216 = 0.333, or 33.3%.
What percentage is that? 26/40 = 0.65, or 65%.

In the baseline condition 26 of 40 obeyed to the end, and in the touch-proximity condition 12 of 40 did. By how many percentage points did obedience fall? 26/40 = 65% and 12/40 = 30%; 65 − 30 = 35 percentage points.
Two bystanders each independently act with probability 0.5. What is the probability, as a percentage, that at least one acts? 1 − 0.5² = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75, or 75%.
What is the probability, as a percentage, that at least one acts? Give one decimal place. P(nobody acts) = 0.8⁵ = 0.32768; P(at least one) = 1 − 0.32768 = 0.67232, or 67.2%.
In a conformity study, 21 of 60 critical answers follow the wrong majority. What percentage conformed? 21/60 = 0.35, or 35%.
Two bystanders each independently act with probability 0.4. What is the probability, as a percentage, that at least one acts? 1 − 0.6² = 1 − 0.36 = 0.64, or 64%.
